### Q-UI-68 · Layout of the application shell and the list screens

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

The owner asked on 2026-10-30 for a product-grade layout with a navigation sidebar, list tables and a filter panel, and supplied a screenshot of another product as a visual reference for layout and interaction only. This decision turns it into trove's own structure; Q-UI-2 (side bar from 1024 CSS px, compact density, container queries) stays in force.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Keep the light side bar and the per-screen tables, restyle with tokens | Same markup, new colours | Smallest change, no new components | Every list screen keeps its own table markup, header handling and filter form; the screens drift again, and the packages list (R-UI-006) would be the ninth copy |
| (b) Dark side bar with folding groups and an icon rail, dark top bar, breadcrumbs from the routes, one data-table component and one filter-panel component on every list screen | The shell of R-UI-002 and the list screens of this change | One look and one keyboard and screen-reader behaviour for the lists; sort, help and states are written once; the packages list and later lists reuse them; the groups keep eleven entries scannable | Two new shared components to maintain; the filter fields move from an always-visible form into a panel that has to be opened |
| (c) A tabbed top navigation with the side bar only inside Administration | Areas as tabs, side bar per area | Familiar from other consoles | Contradicts Q-UI-2 (pinned side bar), hides the second area's entries behind a click, and two navigation designs have to be built and tested |
| (d) A generic grid library for the tables | A third-party grid component | Sorting, resizing and virtual scrolling for free | A new runtime dependency (R-UI-001 asks for none without a reason), its own accessibility and CSP surface, and none of the lists has the thousands of rows that need virtual scrolling: they page through "Load more" |

**Choice:** (b), with these rules. The sidebar and the top bar are dark in both colour schemes, and their text and accent colours are chosen well above the AA minimum of R-UI-044 (the lowest measured pair is 6.3:1 for text and 4.8:1 for the accent mark, against 4.5:1 and 3:1); the content area keeps the Material theme and its one accent, the primary colour. The sidebar's entries are grouped (identity, access, system), carry icons from the icon font (Q-UI-1) and can be compacted to a rail; rail and folded groups are browser-local per principal. Breadcrumbs come from the route configuration. A column is sortable only where the API sorts by it or the whole list is in the browser; a filter exists only where the API takes it; the filter panel applies staged values with one button, and a link that arrives with a filter opens the panel. The top bar's search is the repository list's `q` filter, shown to the callers who may list repositories; the global search waits for its API (R-UI-015).

**Rationale:** The shell and the lists are what an administrator looks at all day, and eight list screens had eight hand-written tables with the same four states each. One component makes the behaviour that is easy to get wrong (an `aria-sort` that follows the sort, a help text that is a real button with a described-by tooltip, a scroll region that is focusable, a sticky header) right once, and it is the reason the packages list can arrive later with the same behaviour at no design cost. (a) leaves that duplication; (c) conflicts with a decision that still holds; (d) buys virtual scrolling that no list needs and costs a dependency. Opening a filter panel costs one click compared with the always-visible form, which is why the toggle shows the number of applied filters and the panel opens by itself when a filter is applied. The development agent revisits this if the walkthrough shows that administrators miss the always-visible filters on the user and token lists (an option would be a pinned panel on wide screens) or when the packages list brings a filter set that does not fit the category pattern.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-002 gains the top bar, grouped navigation, rail, breadcrumbs and list-screen bullets and three acceptance criteria; R-UI-006 states that the packages list uses the shared table and filter panel; R-UI-020 drops "sort by key or creation" (the API has no `sort`; the list is ordered by key) and names the filter panel; R-UI-024, R-UI-025 and R-UI-037 name the sortable column and the panel. The implementation is described in [web-ui.md](../developer/web-ui.md#shell-design-tokens-and-the-list-components).

### Q-UI-69 · Client addresses come from the server's base URL, never from the page's location

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

The repository wizard and the repository page built the client address of a repository from `location.origin`. Behind a proxy, a port forward or another host name for the same installation that origin is not the address a package manager must use; the public base URL is configuration (`server.base_url`, per endpoint `baseUrl`) and the server already serves it. The owner's rule: addresses shown in the UI come from the server's configured base URL.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) `GET /api/v1/system/info` for every screen | `baseUrl` of the installation facts | One call, the value of record | The operation needs `settings:read`; a repository administrator without it would see no address |
| (b) The absolute `addresses` of the repository answers only | Show `addresses[0]` where a repository exists | No permission needed; the server builds them from the same URL | A repository that does not exist yet (the wizard's review step) has no address |
| (c) One service that asks (a) for a holder of `settings:read` and otherwise derives the base from (b), and never from the location | `core/server-address.ts` | Works for every caller who can see any repository; one place to change when the API gains a public base URL | The base is unknown for a caller who may read no repository and may not read the facts; the screens then show no address instead of a wrong one |
| (d) A new public member (login options or `authz/me` carries `baseUrl`) | API change | Works for everyone, including the wizard of the first repository | A change of two contracts outside this work; not needed to fix the defect |

**Choice:** (c). `ServerAddress.baseUrl()` returns the base URL without a trailing slash: from `system/info` when the session holds `settings:read`, else from the first repository (of `GET /api/v1/repositories`, which is filtered by what the caller may see) whose `addresses` has an entry ending in the format's `protocolBasePath` with its key; the part before that suffix is the base. The answer is kept once known and a `null` is not remembered. The wizard and the repository page build the client address from it plus the format's `protocolBasePath` from `GET /api/v1/formats`; the management API addresses of their "as API request" `curl` text come from it too and show `<base URL>` while it is unknown. Where the repository answer carries absolute `addresses` (the list and the consumer view) the screens show them unchanged. `location.origin` is no longer used for any address.

**Rationale:** (a) alone fails a caller the screens are built for (R-AUTHZ-010 gives `repositories:write-config` without `settings:read`), (b) alone has no answer for the wizard, and (d) is the better end state, but it is an API change that the defect does not need. The development agent revisits this when a public member of the base URL exists: `ServerAddress` then reads it, and (c)'s derivation is deleted. The gap that remains today is the wizard of a caller with `repositories:write-config` but neither `settings:read` nor a readable repository: its review shows an en dash for the client address.

**Revisit (done):** [Q-UI-75](#q-ui-75--the-base-url-is-a-member-of-the-formats-answer) added the public member (`baseUrl` of `GET /api/v1/formats`); `ServerAddress` reads it, the derivation from the repository addresses and the call to the installation facts are deleted, and the gap above is closed.

**Applied in the spec:** none (R-REPO-002's address is unchanged); [web-ui.md](../developer/web-ui.md#the-base-url-rule).

### Q-UI-70 · Which clients the install panel and the setup page offer, and where the snippet texts live

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

R-UI-009 and R-UI-016 name the clients (npm, pnpm, Yarn Berry, Yarn Classic; .NET CLI, NuGet CLI, Visual Studio, `nuget.config`). R-API-030 lets the server own the snippets and the UI own the explanations, by `id`.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The UI lists clients per format in one table and the server rejects what it does not know | `features/setup/clients.ts` | A client the server cannot serve never shows; the explanations are translated in the UI | A new client needs a UI release as well as a server one |
| (b) The format descriptor lists its clients | A member of `GET /api/v1/formats` | Both halves change together | A change of the format contract for display data, owned by the repository work package |
| (c) The UI hard-codes npm only | No table | Smallest | No path to NuGet; a second place to edit later |

**Choice:** (a). The table has one entry, npm, with the four clients of R-UI-017 (`npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `yarn-classic`; Q-UI-77 corrected the spelling of Yarn 2 and later); NuGet's clients arrive with the NuGet format (Q-UI-94 adds them). A format that is in the format catalog but not in the table is not offered by the setup page, and the install panel says that there are no instructions yet. The explanation of a snippet is looked up by its `id` (`snippetExplanation`) and is an English source text with a German translation like every other text; an unknown `id` shows the snippet without a sentence. The install panel preselects a virtual repository that holds the version, else the first local one, as R-UI-009 says, and links to `/setup?repository=&client=` with its choice.

**Rationale:** The server must not send prose (R-API-030), and the UI must not parse the snippets. A table in the UI is the smaller coupling of the two. The development agent revisits this when the NuGet format ships: if its clients differ per installation (a Visual Studio entry only where the V2 protocol is on), (b) becomes the better home.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-009 (client picker lists the clients the UI has instructions for).

**Revisited on 2026-10-31:** unchanged for the setup page and the install panel. The format descriptor now lists its clients (Q-API-177), which the guides area of R-UI-049 reads; moving the setup page onto that member stays the revisit at NuGet.

### Q-UI-71 · The README component finishes what Angular's sanitizer leaves

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

R-UI-008 lets the server sanitize and the client bind with `[innerHTML]`, with Angular's sanitizer as the second layer. Reading what that layer actually does showed two gaps: it removes every `id` and `name` (so a `#user-content-…` anchor written by the server's renderer would never exist in the page), and it does not know `vbscript:`.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Trust the two layers as they are | Bind the HTML | No client code | The table-of-contents links of a README are dead; the second layer does not cover `vbscript:` (which no current browser executes, but the rule of R-UI-008 lists it) |
| (b) Bypass the sanitizer with a trusted-HTML value | `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` | The server's ids survive | Forbidden by R-UI-001 and the lint rule; the second layer is gone |
| (c) Bind with the sanitizer, then finish in the component | Walk the bound element once after render: drop disallowed link targets and image sources, set `rel`, derive the heading anchors, keep fragments in the page | Keeps both layers; the added rules are small and testable | The slug rule exists twice (server and client) and must agree |

**Choice:** (c). After binding, the component removes the `href` of an `a` whose target is not a fragment, `http`, `https` or `mailto`; removes an `img` whose source is neither `https` nor a path of this origin; sets `rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer"` and no `target` on every link that leaves trove; gives every heading `id="user-content-<slug>"` (lower case, letters, digits, `_` and `-` kept, spaces to hyphens, a repeated name numbered); and handles a click on a `#user-content-…` link by scrolling inside the README and never navigating. It never builds HTML. The server's renderer must derive the anchors of its table-of-contents links with the same rule (the function `headingSlug` documents it); where the server's links and the client's anchors disagree, the link is dead and no more.

**Rationale:** The client-side finishing can only remove or add attributes of a tree that both layers already cleaned; it cannot introduce a script. Deriving the anchors in the client is the only way to have them at all under the second layer. The development agent revisits this when the server's renderer exists: if it emits ids that Angular's sanitizer keeps (it does not today), the derivation is deleted.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-008 (the client-side finishing, the in-page link behaviour).

### Q-UI-72 · The packages list: tabs, the default view and the created period

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

R-UI-006 asks for three tabs (all, recently viewed, saved views), a default view, filters in the URL and a created period. It does not say where the tab lives, when a default view applies, or how a "last 30 days" view stays right tomorrow.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The tab is the `tab` query parameter; saved views store the query parameters; a default view applies once to an empty query | State in the URL, as the filters | Reload, link and back button keep the tab; saved views are links; the default never overrides a link the user followed | A view stored with `period=30` keeps meaning "30 days", which is the intent |
| (b) Tabs are component state | Local signals | Simplest | A link cannot open "Recently viewed"; reload loses it |
| (c) Saved views store absolute dates | `createdFrom` as a date | Reproducible | A view saved as "last 7 days" would go stale the next day |

**Choice:** (a). Per signed-in principal, browser storage holds the ten last packages opened (`format`, `name`) and at most eight saved views (`id`, name, query) with the id of the default (`trove.packages.<name>`, non-secret, R-UI-043). A relative period is stored as `period=7|30|90` and turned into `createdFrom` when the request is made; a custom period is two days, the end day included (the API's `createdTo` is exclusive, so the request adds one day). Blocked storage, or no signed-in principal, hides the two tabs and ignores `tab=recent|views`. The default view applies once per page load, only when the query has no filter, sort or tab.

**Rationale:** Anything the user could want to send to a colleague belongs in the URL; anything that is a personal shortcut belongs in browser storage and must disappear without it (R-UI-006). The columns first created, versions and downloads of the owner's reference are shown because the API now carries them (Q-API-159); security scanning is not, because trove has no such data. The development agent revisits this if saved views should follow a user across browsers: that needs a server-side preference (R-API-021), which is a contract change.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-006 (columns, sortable columns, the `tab` parameter, the default view).

### Q-UI-73 · The package route is a matcher, and its breadcrumb is one step

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

R-UI-003 gives `/packages/{format}/{name…}`; the name of an npm package may contain one slash (`@team-a/ui`) and the breadcrumb trail of the shell is derived from the route configuration (Q-UI-68).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A matcher route: first segment the format, the rest the name | `packageMatcher` | The path reads like the registry's own; a deep link works; the matcher keeps the slash inside the name | A matcher route has no `path`, so the trail needs a hint |
| (b) A route per depth (`:format/:name` and `:format/:scope/:name`) | Two routes | Plain routes | Maven (`group:artifact`) and later names need more routes; two components to bind |
| (c) The name percent-encoded in one segment | `/packages/npm/%40team-a%2Fui` | One route | Unreadable URLs; `%2F` in a path is refused by proxies |

**Choice:** (a). The file tree's matcher already produces one breadcrumb step per segment; the route data `crumbParam` names a parameter whose value becomes one step instead (a package name is one thing, whatever its slashes). The step links to the page itself; the area steps are "Packages and files" (a name) and "Packages" (the list).

**Rationale:** The trail's job is to answer "where am I"; `@team-a` alone is not a place in trove. The development agent revisits this if scopes become a screen of their own.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-007 (the name keeps its slash and is one breadcrumb step).

### Q-UI-74 · What the setup page does with a token

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

R-UI-016 and R-UI-043 allow three kinds of credentials in the snippets and forbid a token in any shared place. The page has to turn a placeholder into a token without the token travelling.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) One component holds the token in a private signal; composes the snippets from the server's text in a `computed`; discards the token on a change of repository or mode and when the component is destroyed | The page's own state | No shared state, no storage, no URL; the server never sees a pasted value | The token disappears on reload, by design |
| (b) A setup service keeps the token for the steps | A root service | Survives navigation inside the page | A token in a shared service is the thing R-UI-043 forbids |
| (c) The server composes the snippets with the token | The token goes up and comes back | No client work | The server must never fill a token (R-API-030) |

**Choice:** (a). `fillToken` replaces every `{{token}}` literally (a `$&` in a token means nothing). A pasted value is checked in the browser for prefix, length, alphabet and the CRC-32 of INV-8 (`checkTokenShape`, tested with the test vector of R-AUTH-022 and with a flip of every character), the field is a password input with a reveal toggle, `autocomplete="off"` and `spellcheck="false"`; only a value that passes reaches the snippets; no request is made for it. "Create a token" asks for a personal token with the description "Client setup: <client>, <repository>, <date>", the scope `read` on the chosen repository (and `read` plus `deploy` on the setup answer's `publishTarget` when the user ticks the publish option), and the lifetime `tokenTtlSeconds`; it keeps one `Idempotency-Key` per setup and handles the lost-answer case (409 `token_already_issued`) as the token screen does. The token is shown once in a status region with a copy button. A file with a token is offered through a Blob URL revoked right after the click.

**Rationale:** The token is the page's secret; the cheapest way to keep it from leaking is to give it one owner that dies with the route. The CRC check is not a security measure (R-AUTH-022): it catches a truncated paste before the user writes a broken file. The development agent revisits this if the dialog form (R-UI-029's one-time display) becomes a shared component: then this page uses it and its own display of the created token is deleted.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-016 (credentials step, the pasted-token checks, the created token's scope and lifetime).

### Q-UI-75 · The base URL is a member of the formats answer

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Q-UI-69 chose to derive the client address from the repository addresses for a caller without `settings:read` and named the gap that remained: the wizard of a caller with `repositories:write-config` who may neither read the installation facts nor any repository showed an en dash for the client address. It also named the end state: a public member of the base URL, after which the derivation is deleted. The client setup of R-API-030 needs the same address for every caller who may read a repository, including a caller whose only readable repository is not in the first page of the list.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) `baseUrl` in `GET /api/v1/authz/me` | The answer about the caller carries the address | One call at sign-in | The operation is the caller's own rights; an address is not one; an anonymous caller gets a different, shorter answer |
| (b) `baseUrl` in `GET /api/v1/formats` | The format catalog carries the base URL its path templates are joined with | The two halves of a client address (`protocolBasePath` and the base) arrive in one answer that every caller may read and that every screen building an address already asks for; no new operation | The catalog is a list of formats, and gains a member that is not about a format |
| (c) A new operation `GET /api/v1/system/base-url` | A resource of its own | A clean place | Another operation, another permission declaration and another fake for three lines of data |
| (d) Keep the derivation of Q-UI-69 | No API change | Nothing to do | The gap stays; a caller with a first page of repositories it may not match gets no address |

**Choice:** (b). `FormatList` gains the required member `baseUrl`: the configured base URL of the endpoint the request arrived on (`server.base_url`, or the base URL of the further endpoint), an origin without a trailing slash, or `null` when none is configured. The member is read from the request's resolved information only when its source is the configuration; an address built from the `Host` of the request (development only) is never handed out. `ServerAddress.baseUrl()` reads it through `RepositoriesApi.baseUrl()`; the derivation from repository addresses, the call to the installation facts and the dependency on `settings:read` are deleted. A `null` is not remembered.

**Rationale:** The base URL is no secret: it is the address every client of every repository is configured with, and `GET /api/v1/formats` is open to every caller that may use the UI at all. Putting it next to `protocolBasePath` makes the join the only thing a screen does. The development agent revisits this when a format-independent public information operation exists (login options already are one, before sign-in); the member then moves there.

**Applied in the spec:** R-API-022 (the row of `GET /api/v1/formats`: the `baseUrl` member); [web-ui.md](../developer/web-ui.md#the-base-url-rule). Closes the gap named in Q-UI-69.

### Q-UI-76 · One rule for the heading anchors, checked on both sides by one corpus

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

The server writes the table-of-contents links of a README as `#user-content-<slug>` (R-UI-008) and the component derives the anchor of every heading again, because Angular's sanitizer removes every `id` (Q-UI-71). Two implementations of one rule in two languages differ in the corners: JavaScript's `trim`, `\s` and `toLowerCase` are not Go's `TrimSpace`, `unicode.IsSpace` and `strings.ToLower` (U+0085 is white space for Go and not for JavaScript, U+FEFF the other way round; Go has no final-sigma rule and maps U+0130 to a plain `i`). A heading with one of them gets an anchor that the table of contents does not point to.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Both sides use their language's functions | Ordinary Go and TypeScript | Least code | The two differ for white space and for case, silently |
| (b) The server writes the anchors and the component keeps them | No second derivation | One rule | Angular's sanitizer removes the `id`; the component cannot keep what it never receives, unless the sanitizer is bypassed, which R-UI-008 forbids |
| (c) The server implements JavaScript's functions and both sides test one corpus | `jsSpace`, `jsLower` and `finalSigma` in `internal/packages/readme`; the same 35-entry table in the Go test and in the component's spec | The rule is the browser's, because the browser has the last word; a difference fails a test on the side that moved | Forty lines of Go that restate parts of ECMAScript |

**Choice:** (c). `readme.HeadingSlug` trims and lower-cases the way JavaScript does and replaces what JavaScript's `\s` matches by a hyphen; the table `slugCorpus` (`internal/packages/readme/render_test.go`) and `SLUG_CORPUS` (`web/src/app/features/packages/package-readme.spec.ts`) hold the same headings with the anchors that Node.js 26 produced; a change to the rule or to either table is made in both.

**Rationale:** A table of contents whose links miss their headings is a defect users see on the first README with a non-ASCII heading. The corpus costs one table, and the Greek and Turkish corners it contains are the ones a text function of another language gets wrong. The development agent revisits this when the component stops deriving the anchors (a sanitizer that keeps `user-content-` ids).

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-008 (the heading rule in the bullet on the component's finishing pass).

### Q-UI-77 · The client ids of the setup screens are the format's

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

R-API-030 and Q-UI-70 spelled the clients of npm `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn-berry` and `yarn-classic`. The npm format registers `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn` and `yarn-classic` as its clients (`Descriptor.Clients`) and as the `Client` of its setup templates (R-NPM-041), and the setup answer is rendered from those templates.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The server accepts `yarn-berry` and maps it to `yarn` | An alias table | The UI stays as written | A second spelling of every client forever; the format owns its client ids |
| (b) The UI uses the format's ids | `yarn` for Yarn 2 and later; the label stays "Yarn Berry (2 and later)" | One spelling; the snippet ids (`yarn.configure.yarnrc`) already are `yarn…` | A rename in the UI table, its explanations and its fakes |

**Choice:** (b). The client ids are the format's own; the UI's table of clients per format (Q-UI-70) lists `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn` and `yarn-classic`, and an unknown value answers `400 malformed_request` naming the clients the format serves.

**Rationale:** The format page is the source of its client list (R-API-030); the UI table only decides what the pickers offer. The development agent revisits this when a format's client id needs a display name the UI cannot derive from the server (the catalog already carries `DisplayName` per client).

**Applied in the spec:** R-API-030 (the client list of npm), R-UI-017.

### Q-UI-78 · The repository settings form renders the subset of JSON Schema the formats use

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: R-UI-021 and R-ARCH-004 render a format's settings from the schema `GET /api/v1/formats` serves (`settingsSchema`, Q-ARCH-229); Q-UI-18 had left the forms hand-built for the generic format, so the `npm` member could be set through the API only. npm's schema holds booleans and string enums, each with a default and its classes in `x-trove-classes`; the audit settings of R-NPM-038 add an object of the remote class with an enum, a nullable URL, and durations and byte sizes written as strings. The server compiles and enforces the whole schema.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A renderer of the subset the formats use, in the repository feature | An object with `properties` is a fieldset, `boolean` a checkbox, `enum` a select, `string` a text field (`format: uri` a URL field), `integer` and `number` a text field with a numeric keyboard; `null` in a type list is ignored, so an empty field means "not set"; a member whose `x-trove-classes` lack the class is left out at every level; any other construct (an array, a composition, `$ref`) is shown with its stored value and "Set it through the API" | No dependency (INV-1); a format adds a setting by editing its schema; the server stays the only validator | A construct outside the subset is not editable until the renderer learns it |
| (b) A JSON Schema form library | A generic form engine | Covers more of the standard | A dependency with its own widgets, styles and accessibility for four switches today; its validation would be a second one next to the server's |
| (c) A panel per format under `features/formats/<id>/` | Hand-written controls | Free layout | Code per field, which R-ARCH-004 reserves for what a schema cannot express; the schema and the panel drift apart |

**Choice:** (a): the model is `features/repositories/settings-schema.ts` (`settingNodes`, `pruneDefaults`), the component `format-settings.ts`. The form does not validate: a number field sends a number only when its text is one as JSON writes it, otherwise the text, which the server refuses at the field (`invalid_value`). A server field error goes to the control of the deepest member its pointer names, else to the enclosing object or to the section, in the field and in the error summary.

**Rationale:** The settings the formats declare are switches and choices; a renderer of that subset is small and keeps every control a labelled native element (Q-UI-14). The development agent revisits this when a format's schema needs a construct the subset lacks (a list of strings, a `oneOf`) and then extends the renderer, not the format.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-021 (where the settings appear, an acceptance criterion); the "Settings forms" row of Q-UI-18 is superseded for the format member.

### Q-UI-79 · The labels and descriptions of the settings form are the schema's

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: every UI text is translatable (R-UI-045), while a schema's descriptions are English texts of the format; a translation per member would be code per field.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The schema's texts as sent | The label is the schema's `title`, else the member name (`latestGuard`), the name the API tab and the `curl` text show; the description is shown as the schema has it, marked `lang="en"`; enum values are shown as they are written | R-UI-045 keeps API texts English and identifiers untranslated; a new setting needs no UI change | German users read English descriptions, and npm's descriptions carry requirement IDs written for the API reader |
| (b) A translation table in the UI keyed by format and member | `$localize` per member | German texts | Code per field (R-ARCH-004); a schema change without a UI change shows an untranslated member anyway |
| (c) Localized schemas from the server | `title` and `description` per locale | Both languages without UI code | A server change and a second text per member in every format, for four settings |

**Choice:** (a). The texts the form adds itself ("Default: on", "Not set", the introduction, the note on a construct it does not edit, the step and tab names) are translated.

**Rationale:** The settings are configuration identifiers that an administrator meets again in the API and in the format's documentation; the description explains them in the language the API speaks. The development agent revisits this when the owner wants German descriptions or a format writes its schema for end users: (c) would then keep the text with the format. Walkthrough note: whether the descriptions should lose their requirement IDs is the format's choice (its schema), not the form's.

**Applied in the spec:** none; R-UI-045 already keeps API texts English.

### Q-UI-80 · A setting equal to its default is not written

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: a checkbox and a select always show a value, so for an absent setting the form shows the schema's default. What does the form send when the value shown is the default?

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Leave it out | The format member carries only the settings that differ from their default; an object that this leaves empty is left out, and so is the member; a `required` member and a member the schema does not know stay | The repository follows the format's default (Q-NPM-59: an omitted setting takes its default); switching a value back and forth is no change; the create body is minimal | A value deliberately set to today's default is not pinned |
| (b) Write every effective value | The form fills in the defaults | The document states everything | Every repository the form touches pins today's defaults, and a later default changes nothing for them |
| (c) Write what the user touched | Touched members are written as set | Pins what was chosen | A switch set back is an unsaved change; the dirty check needs a record of touched members |

**Choice:** (a). The edit form compares the stored and the edited member both without their defaults, so a stored explicit default is no change, and a value set back to its default sends `null` for it, or for the whole member, in the merge patch.

**Rationale:** The format owns its defaults (Q-NPM-59); a form that wrote them would freeze them into every repository it saves. The development agent revisits this when a format has a setting whose default may change but must stay as it is for existing repositories; such a setting is `required` in the schema, which (a) keeps.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-021.

### Q-UI-81 · The format settings are a section of the class-specific step and a tab of the edit form

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: R-UI-021 has five steps (class, format, basic settings, class-specific settings, review), and the edit form shows the same sections as tabs. Each member of npm's schema applies to one class.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A section of the fourth step and a tab of its own | When the schema has a member for the class, the fourth step shows a section "npm settings" below the access settings and is called "Access and npm settings"; the review lists the settings that will be written, or "The defaults of the format"; the edit form has a tab "npm settings" between Access and API | Five steps as specified; the settings are class-specific by construction; a format without settings shows nothing new | The name of the step changes once a format is chosen |
| (b) A sixth step "Format settings" | A step of its own, only when there are members | A clear place | The number of steps depends on the format; R-UI-021 names five |
| (c) Part of the basic settings | Next to the key and the description | One step less | The basic step does not depend on the class, the settings do |

**Choice:** (a). Choosing another class or format in the wizard starts the format settings afresh, because a member of another class would be refused (`not_applicable`).

**Rationale:** The schema already sorts its members by class, which is what the class-specific step is for. The development agent revisits the layout when a format's settings outgrow one section (more than about ten controls) and would then give them a step of their own. Walkthrough note: the owner should look at the step name and at the tab between Access and API.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-021.

### Q-UI-82 · The packages journey compares the setup page with the matrix's snippet written out

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: E2.8 asks that E2.1's configure step use the snippets of the client setup dialog verbatim. The npm matrix does not open the dialog: `setupSnippet` ([npm_matrix_test.go](../../test/e2e/npm_matrix_test.go)) renders npm's configure templates with the data the setup API would give them (the edge's registry URL on `localhost`, the keyed credential line with `${TROVE_TOKEN}`, the always-auth switches of a repository that is not anonymously readable). R-UI-047's acceptance criterion asks that a deliberately broken snippet template fail the client-setup journey.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The journey compares the page with the snippet written out for the matrix's data | `matrixSnippet` in `web/e2e/tests/08-packages.spec.ts` spells out what the templates render for the journey's repository; the snippet on the page must equal it character for character, for each of the four clients, with the file it names | A broken template fails the journey (R-UI-047); page, API and matrix are held against one independent statement | The rendering is written down a second time: a deliberate template change edits the journey too |
| (b) The journey compares the page with the setup API's answer | `GET /api/v1/repositories/{repoKey}/client-setup` with the administrator token | Nothing written twice | Proves only that the page shows what the API says; a broken template passes |
| (c) The matrix opens the dialog | The Go test drives a browser | The literal criterion | A browser in the npm suite for text the API already returns |

**Choice:** (a), with the credential mode "Reference an environment variable", which writes `${TROVE_TOKEN}` as the matrix does. The journey's repository is its own local npm repository (INV-17: prepared through the API), not `npm-all`, which only the npm suite creates; the templates are the same for every key.

**Rationale:** The criterion exists to catch a dialog and a client configuration that disagree, and only an expected text that neither of them produced can. The development agent revisits this when the matrix reads its snippets from the setup API itself, which would make (b) enough.

**Applied in the spec:** none; [e2e.md](../developer/e2e.md#browser-journeys) describes the journey.

instructions of later formats at P1. Nothing in the UI said what a local, a remote or a virtual repository is, how a

| (b) An in-app guide per variant (format × class × client), in the beta, and every later format ships its own | R-UI-049, R-API-053; R-UI-019 raised | Every variant is explained where it is used | One more surface each format keeps true |

**Choice:** (b).

**Rationale:** the owner's decision. The development agent records no revisit condition; the scope is the owner's.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-049 and R-API-053 (new, MVP); R-UI-019 (raised to MVP: every format ships its guide in

### Q-UI-84 · Where the guides appear

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: a developer looks for help in two situations: before choosing a repository ("what is a virtual repository?")
and while looking at one ("how do I publish to this one?"). The setup page already holds the snippets and the token
handling of R-UI-016.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A second step of the setup page | One page | Everything in one place | The setup page grows a manual, and its token handling becomes part of every reading of the docs |
| (b) A guides area in the side bar, a How to use tab on the repository screen, links between both and the setup page | `/guides`, the tab, the links carry format, client and repository | Reachable before and while using a repository; the setup page stays the place where a token is handled | Two entry points to keep consistent; both use one component |
| (c) Help links to an external site | `ui.help_url` | Nothing to build | Not the installation's addresses or behaviour; no such site exists (Q-UI-15) |

**Choice:** (b). The area is in Packages and files, visible to every caller (anonymous ones included where anonymous access is on). The tab sits before the API tab of the edit form, and the consumer view shows the same guide below its facts. The guides area offers the formats of `GET /api/v1/formats` with clients, so NuGet appears without a screen change.

**Rationale:** The guide is reading, the setup page is doing; keeping them apart keeps the token in one component (Q-UI-74). The development agent revisits this when a global help button exists (R-UI-002's help link), which would then open the guides area.

### Q-UI-85 · A guide section is bound like a README, with the setup snippets below it

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the server renders a section's Markdown with the README renderer (Q-API-178). Angular's sanitizer removes the heading ids, and a bare fragment link navigates to the UI root because of the document's `<base href>` (Q-UI-71).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Bind the HTML with the README component and render the snippets as structured data | `trove-package-readme` per section; snippets with copy buttons | The one finishing pass of Q-UI-71 serves both; the snippets are copied exactly as the setup page shows them | One README component instance per section |
| (b) Put the snippets into the Markdown as code blocks | One HTML string | One binding | No copy button, and the snippet is no longer the setup API's value but a rendering of it |
| (c) A component of its own for guide HTML | A second finishing pass | Freedom | Two implementations of one sanitizing rule |

**Choice:** (a). The contents list is a `nav` landmark whose links move the focus to the section's heading and never navigate. The snippets have a copy button and no download: a guide holds no secret, and downloading is the setup page's.

**Rationale:** The guide must show exactly what the setup page shows; structured snippets make that a comparison of values, not of renderings. The development agent revisits this when a section needs an interactive element the sanitizer cannot carry.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-049.

### Q-UI-88 · The design language and its two colour schemes

Status: **The owner's requirement of 2026-11-01; the adaptation decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough. **Superseded in part by [Q-UI-96](#q-ui-96--cogpit-blue-as-the-primary-colour-green-only-for-positive-status)**: the accent is cogpit's blue (light `#0a62c2`, dark `#4aa8ff`) instead of the screens' green, and green marks a positive status only; the surfaces, borders, chrome and type stay as chosen here.

Context: the owner sent two example screens, one dark and one light, and asked that trove take their design language and
colours, with a dark and a light mode. The measured values and the reading of both screens are in
[design-language.md](../developer/design-language.md). Two measured values miss WCAG AA, which R-UI-044 requires and the
browser tier checks with axe's `color-contrast` rule: the accent green as text or as the fill under white text on the
white page (2.8:1), and the muted grey of the dark screen on its cards (4.1:1).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The measured values everywhere | Green `#3db064` on white, grey `#737984` on dark cards | Closest to the screens | Fails R-UI-044 and the axe check of the browser tier |
| (b) The measured values, with the tones that miss AA moved in their own hue | Light scheme: accent `#1a6e3c` (6.3:1 on white and under white text, 5.1:1 on the filled form field), muted text `#5b6270`; dark scheme: accent `#3db064` as measured (7.1:1), muted text `#9aa1ad` (6.9:1); surfaces, borders, chrome as measured | The screens' look with readable text; one place (`main.scss`) holds the palette | The light scheme's green is darker than the screen's |
| (c) Material tonal palettes generated from the two seed colours | Only `primary` and `neutral` as input | No hand-set values | Surfaces and chrome come out far from the screens (Material's dark surface is a neutral grey, not the screens' near-black navy) |

**Choice:** (b). The theme button moves out of the user menu into the top bar, as on the dark example screen, and keeps
the third choice "Follow the system" (R-API-021). The type stays the system font stack: the screens use a humanist sans,
and a self-hosted web font would add files to the bundle for a difference most readers will not see.

**Rationale:** The design language is the screens' structure and surfaces as much as their hue, so the surfaces, borders
and chrome are taken as measured; only the two text tones move, by the least step that passes AA. The development agent
revisits the type when the walkthrough finds the system font out of keeping, and every tone when the owner prefers the
screens' green to the contrast rule.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-002; [design-language.md](../developer/design-language.md);
[web-ui.md](../developer/web-ui.md#design-tokens).

### Q-UI-89 · How the manual reaches the UI

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the owner wants the user and administrator documentation delivered by the frontend (R-UI-050). The server already
renders and sanitizes Markdown for READMEs and guides (R-UI-008, R-API-053), and the UI binds that HTML with one component.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Markdown in the repository, embedded into the binary, rendered by the server's README renderer, read through two operations | `docs/manual/`, `internal/manual`, R-API-054 | One renderer and sanitizer for every Markdown text; the manual is the running version's; works without internet; links checked by a Go test | Two operations and a load step at start-up |
| (b) HTML rendered at build time into the UI's assets | A build step with a Markdown library | No API | A second Markdown pipeline beside the server's, a second sanitizer policy to keep equal, the build grows a step |
| (c) Markdown fetched as assets and rendered in the browser | A Markdown library in the bundle | No server change | A dependency and its weight in the bundle; the browser's sanitizer only |
| (d) A link to a documentation site | `ui.help_url` (Q-UI-15) | Nothing to build | No such site exists; it would describe another version than the installation runs, and an air-gapped installation cannot reach it |

**Choice:** (a). Links between pages are relative `.md` links, so the same files read on GitHub; the server turns them into
links of the help area, and a link to a page or heading that does not exist stops the load.

**Rationale:** The manual is the third Markdown text trove shows; giving it the pipeline the other two use keeps one
sanitizer policy and one binding component, and embedding it ties the text to the version it describes. The development
agent revisits this if the manual needs content per installation (addresses, configured providers), which the guides of
R-API-053 already cover for package clients.

**Applied in the spec:** R-API-054, R-UI-050; [architecture.md](architecture.md) R-ARCH-003 (the packages).
