### Q-UI-140 · Which file names of the UI build are hashed

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: R-UI-001 caches hashed assets as immutable, and the shared asset store of
[ha-and-helm.md](ha-and-helm.md#q-ha-120--how-a-replica-serves-a-hashed-ui-file-of-the-other-release) may serve nothing else. The
server's pattern was `-[A-Z0-9]{8}.<ext>`, the names of esbuild (`main-6E6OBYEH.js`). The Angular 22 build names its chunks with
eight base64url characters of either case (`chunk-Bo__WLzq.js`, `chunk-b3RHWPW-.js`): in a build of 2026-11-06 130 of the 131 chunks of a
locale did not match, were served `no-cache` and would not have been published. The hash covers the code before the translations
are inlined: the locales of one build share every name, and most of the files differ between them.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) One pattern for server and build, checked at build time (chosen) | `<name>-<8 of [A-Za-z0-9_-]>.<extension of 1 to 8>` in at most two plain directories ([hashed.go](../../internal/webui/hashed.go)); `build:embed` fails when a file other than `index.html` and the copies of `public/` does not match, or such a copy does ([hashed.mjs](../../web/scripts/hashed.mjs)); a unit test keeps the two patterns equal | The chunks are cached and shareable; a change of the builder's names fails the build instead of a rolling upgrade; a file is named by locale and path everywhere | The pattern is a contract with the builder that has to follow its next change |
| (b) A manifest of hashed files written by the build | The server reads the list | Exact | Angular's builder writes none; it would be a second output to keep in sync |
| (c) Keep the upper-case pattern | No change | — | The chunks stay `no-cache` and cannot be served across an upgrade |

**Choice:** (a).

**Rationale:** the server and the build agree on one rule, and the build is where a disagreement is found first. Revisit when the
builder changes its hash format: `build:embed` says so.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-001 (serving), [docs/developer/web-ui.md](../developer/web-ui.md). Tests: `TestIsHashed`,
`TestChunkCaching`, `TestHashedPatternOfTheBuild`.

### Q-UI-141 · What a replica answers for a hashed file of another release

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: a request for a hashed file that the replica's build lacks is looked up in the shared asset store
([ha-and-helm.md](ha-and-helm.md#q-ha-120--how-a-replica-serves-a-hashed-ui-file-of-the-other-release)). The answer has to be one a
browser handles, for a file that exists, one that does not and a store that cannot be asked.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The file, `404`, or `503` (chosen) | A file from the store has the headers of the replica's own (type by extension, `nosniff`, immutable); a name no release published is `404` problem+json; a store that cannot be asked is `503` problem+json with `Retry-After: 1` and `Cache-Control: no-store`, logged. A replica keeps the files it read in memory (32 MiB at most, the oldest out first, read again after an hour, Q-UI-142), remembers an unknown name for 10 s (4,096 names at most), and reads a file once for concurrent requests; a read is bounded by 10 s and always verified (Q-UI-143) | A browser caches a found file as its own; the `503` says the file may exist and is never cached; repeated requests cost one read | Memory per replica for the files of the other release; a name published within 10 s of a miss is found 10 s later on that replica |
| (b) `404` when the store cannot be asked | One answer for every miss | Simple | Says the file does not exist; a heuristic cache may keep it |
| (c) Forward the request to a replica of the other release | A proxy hop | No store | Needs an address per release, a second hop, and nothing for a release whose replicas are gone (the open tab) |

**Choice:** (a).

**Rationale:** the answers say what is true about the file. A file of a hashed name never changes its code, so a kept copy differs
from the store's at most in translated strings (Q-UI-142), and the memory is the bound of a working set of one release's bundle
(about 5 MB in two locales). Revisit if the files of
more than one other release are read in one window.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-001 (serving), [docs/developer/web-ui.md](../developer/web-ui.md). Code:
[shared.go](../../internal/webui/shared.go). Tests: `TestSharedAssets`, `TestSharedCacheBound`, and
`TestR_HA_020_SharedUIAssetsWithoutTheObjectStore`.

### Q-UI-142 · Which bytes the shared store keeps for a name that two builds fill differently

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the hash in a file's name covers the code before the translations are inlined
([Q-UI-140](#q-ui-140--which-file-names-of-the-ui-build-are-hashed)), so a release that changes only a German string keeps the
chunk's name and changes its `de` bytes. The store has one row per `(locale, path)`, because the URL a page asks for names no build.
The first design kept the first publisher's row for good, renewed it by name from every build that had the name, and never replaced
a row whose blob was damaged: a row could hold the bytes of a release that no longer ran, and a lost object answered `503` on every
replica that lacked the file until the retention ended (review of 2026-11-06).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The row of the bytes that run: renewed by content, replaced when stale or damaged (chosen) | A replica renews only the rows that hold its own bytes (`TouchUIAssets` compares the digest), counts as present only a row with its bytes and a live, `ok` blob, and its insert replaces a row with other bytes when that row's blob is not live and `ok`, or when no replica whose build has those bytes renewed it for `shared.StaleAfter` (2 h, twice the renewal); the update trigger queues the old blob. A replica keeps a file it read for an hour, then reads it again (on a store that cannot be asked it serves the kept copy on) | While two releases with different bytes for a name run side by side, the row stays with the one that wrote it, so the rows do not flip; within about three hours after a release's last replica stopped, the name holds the bytes of a build that still runs; a damaged row is replaced or repaired at the next renewal of any build that has the name | During the window a replica that lacks the name serves one release's bytes to the pages of both; a missing object that no check has marked yet still answers `503` until the blob check of R-STOR-013 marks it |
| (b) First writer, for good | As built first | Stable | Keeps the bytes of a release that no longer runs as long as any build renews the name, and a damaged blob for good |
| (c) Last writer | Every publish replaces a row with other bytes | The newest bytes | Two releases that run side by side replace each other's row every hour |
| (d) A row per build | The key holds the digest | Every build's bytes kept | The request names no build, so the replica still has to pick one; more rows for nothing |

**Choice:** (a). For the window itself nothing better is possible than one release's bytes per name: the URL is the same for both,
and a browser that loaded the file once keeps it for a year (`immutable`) whichever release's page asks for it later. The bytes differ
in translated strings, not in code, because a code change changes the name.

**Rationale:** the store follows the builds that run, as the retention of Q-HA-122 does, and a damaged row heals instead of waiting
out the retention. Revisit if a build's translation must be exact on every replica during an upgrade: that needs names that cover the
translated bytes, a change of the build, not of the store.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-001 (serving), [ha-and-helm.md](ha-and-helm.md) Q-HA-122. Code: the statements `UIAssetsPresent`,
`InsertUIAsset` and `TouchUIAssets` of [ui_assets.sql](../../internal/meta/postgres/queries/ui_assets.sql), `Publish` in
[shared.go](../../internal/webui/shared/shared.go), `sharedFileTTL` in [internal/webui/shared.go](../../internal/webui/shared.go).
Tests: `TestR_HA_020_SharedUIAssets` (a name two builds fill with other bytes; a row whose blob is damaged), `TestSharedAssets`.

### Q-UI-143 · A file of the shared store is verified whatever storage.download.verify says

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: `storage.download.verify: false` (R-STOR-013, Q-STOR-6) hands out an object's bytes unchecked. For a package file that is
the operator's choice; a file of the shared store is served from trove's origin as script, kept in a replica's memory and cached by
browsers as immutable, so an object replaced in the bucket with bytes of the same length would run as trove's code (review of
2026-11-06).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Always verify this path (chosen) | `blob.OpenOptions.Verify` verifies a full read whatever the setting; the store asks for it and checks the length and the SHA-256 of the buffered bytes once more; a mismatch marks the blob corrupt as every verified read does, and the request answers `503` | A writer of the bucket alone cannot put code into the UI; the cost is a hash of at most 8 MiB per file and replica, kept in memory afterwards | None of weight: the files are small and read rarely |
| (b) Follow the setting | As before | One rule | The setting would decide whether the bucket can inject script into trove's origin |

**Choice:** (a).

**Rationale:** the setting trades a hash for speed on large downloads; it was never meant to decide what runs in the browser.
Revisit if a file of the store can exceed `shared.MaxFileSize`.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-001 (serving), [docs/security/ui-asset-store.md](../security/ui-asset-store.md). Code:
`OpenOptions.Verify` in [download.go](../../internal/blob/download.go), `readVerified` in
[shared.go](../../internal/webui/shared/shared.go). Tests: `TestDownloadVerification` (a swapped object with verification off),
`TestReadVerified`.

### Q-UI-144 · Where the notices of the bundled software are served

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the font licence of Inter (OFL-1.1) asks that its notice travel with the font, and the icon font is Apache-2.0, which needs
its licence text with the redistribution. The build of 2026-11-06 writes Angular's `3rdpartylicenses.txt` to `web/dist/web/`, next
to `browser/`, so it was not in the locale directories the binary embeds. The file names `@fontsource-variable/inter` with OFL-1.1
and has no entry for `material-icons`: the icon font's stylesheet (`material-icons/iconfont/outlined.css`) has no comment and no
licence text, so there is nothing for the extraction to collect.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) One copy per locale, `/ui/<locale>/3rdpartylicenses.txt` (chosen) | `build:embed` writes Angular's file and the icon font's licence into each locale directory, after the hashed-name check; the handler serves it as any file of the locale | No new code path: the handler's file rule (R-UI-001) serves it; every UI file lives under `/ui/<locale>/`, and the link of a page resolves through its base href | Two identical copies in the binary (about 38 KB each); the address names a locale |
| (b) One address, `/ui/3rdpartylicenses.txt`, for every locale | A case of `webui.ServeHTTP` before the locale redirect, and an exception to the rule that `/ui/` paths carry a locale | One address for all languages | A new form of path under `/ui/`, and a code path and a test of its own; the text is English in every locale anyway |
| (c) An endpoint of the management API | A route in the API's surface and the OpenAPI document | The API's conventions | A notice is not an API resource; it adds an operation for a static file |

**Choice:** (a).

**Rationale:** the notices are the same English text in both locales, so the copies cost binary size and nothing else, while the
handler, the cache rules and the content type (`.txt` is `text/plain; charset=utf-8`) already exist. The notices are not hashed, so
the shared asset store does not publish them (`Store.Asset` and `Store.Publish` take hashed names only), and a rolling upgrade
serves each release's own notices from its own replicas. The link sits on the Installation card of the system status (R-UI-038),
next to the version it belongs to, and the manual names the address for everyone, including people without `settings:read`.
Revisit if an address that does not depend on the locale must be cited from outside the UI (then (b)), or if the notices grow
beyond what two copies in the binary cost.

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-001 (serving), R-UI-038 (the Installation card). Documented in
[web-ui.md](../developer/web-ui.md#how-the-build-reaches-the-binary), [design-language.md](../developer/design-language.md) and the
[manual](../manual/admin/overview.md#one-binary-several-roles). Code: [build-embed.mjs](../../web/scripts/build-embed.mjs),
[system-status.html](../../web/src/app/features/system/system-status.html). Tests: `TestR_UI_001_ThirdPartyNotices`
([notices_test.go](../../internal/webui/notices_test.go)), and `R-UI-038 Q-UI-144` in
[system-status.spec.ts](../../web/src/app/features/system/system-status.spec.ts).

### Q-UI-145 · The logo's wordmark as paths from Inter Bold, and a reduced mark as the favicon

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the logo's wordmark was SVG `<text>` in the system font, so the lockup and the app icon rendered in another face per
platform; at 16 px the three lanes of the mark ran together, and `favicon.ico` was the framework's default icon. Two open
points of the logo (the third, removing the drafts and the preview, waits for the owner to call the logo final).

How the outlines are made, in `web/scripts/brand-logo.mjs` (the generator stays the one source):

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) opentype.js on the static Inter Bold file (chosen) | Dev dependencies `opentype.js` and `@fontsource/inter`, both pinned exactly; the script reads `inter-latin-700-normal.woff` and writes one `<path class="word">` per lockup, with the font's advances and the tracking of the `<text>` | The weight is a parameter of the generator (a file name); no path data to keep in step; the font is the release the UI ships, as a static file of the same package family | Two dev dependencies (neither is shipped: the build does not import them) |
| (b) fontkit on the variable `.woff2` of `@fontsource-variable/inter` | One font package already in the tree | No second font package | Tried and dropped: fontkit's WOFF2 reader fails on `getVariation` and applies no variation to the outlines of a transformed `glyf` table, so it yields the regular weight only without patching its private API |
| (c) Generate the paths once, commit them as constants | No dependency | Nothing to install | The tool that made them is not in the repo; a change of weight, size or spacing means redoing a manual step |

**Choice (outlines):** (a). Not verified: the pair kerning of the static file is read through `Font.getKerningValue`, which
returns 0 for the pairs of "trove"; the spacing is the advances plus the 6 and 4 unit tracking the `<text>` had.

How the favicon is made:

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The mark reduced to two lanes, thicker strokes, on the app icon's dark tile; SVG and ICO (chosen) | Band 48 and lanes of 34 units (of 256) in the candidate's blue and red, the red one still curving out from beneath the blue; the tile is the same in both schemes; `favicon.svg` plus `favicon.ico` with PNG frames of 16, 32 and 48 px, both generated | The v, the split and the curve survive at 16 px; the tab's colour does not decide the contrast; the ICO is what the setup had, so it stays as the fallback | The favicon is a tile, the mark in the lockup is not |
| (b) The full mark scaled down, no tile | No second form | Nothing to maintain | The three lanes run together at 16 px, the reason for the task |
| (c) The reduced mark without a tile, following `prefers-color-scheme` | Same as the lockup | One look for the logo | The ICO fallback cannot follow the scheme; neutral on a light or dark tab bar needs two files |

**Choice (favicon):** (a). The ICO's frames are rasterised by the generator itself (distance to the flattened lane paths, 8 by 8
samples per pixel, PNG through `node:zlib`), so no image tool is a dependency and the output is deterministic.

**Rationale:** the wordmark's face is a property of the brand, not of the viewer's platform; the favicon is read at 16 px, where
the mark's detail is below a pixel, so the form is drawn for that size. Revisit when the owner changes the weight or the lane
count of the mark (the reduced form takes its own parameters in the script), or when `@fontsource-variable/inter` ships static
files or fontkit instances WOFF2 outlines (then (b) drops the second font package).

**Applied in the spec:** the [design language's logo section](../developer/design-language.md#logo). Code:
`wordPath`, `faviconSvg`, `faviconPixels` in [brand-logo.mjs](../../web/scripts/brand-logo.mjs); the icons in
[index.html](../../web/src/index.html); `.svg` content type in `contentType` of [webui.go](../../internal/webui/webui.go).

### Q-UI-148 · A link in a table or a key-value list is its own box, and the language submenu opens on a click

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the owner's review (Q-UI-128) set links in tables and key-value lists to "underlined only under the pointer and on
focus". axe's `link-in-text-block` (WCAG 1.4.1, colour as the only mark) then fired in the browser journeys on the package
page's Vulnerabilities tab: a row header with the advisory link and the summary as an inline span after it is a link in a
block of text, and the link blue is 1.5:1 against the text. Other cells have the same shape (a link and a badge, a link and a
hint, a link and a path). The same review replaced the Material menu by the CDK menu, whose submenu opens when the pointer
enters its trigger and toggles on click, so the click of a pointer user, whose pointer is already on the item, closed the
submenu the hover had just opened (journey 07, R-UI-045).

How a link in a table or a key-value list stays clear of the rule:

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The link is an inline-block box there (chosen) | One rule for `.content :is(table, dl) a`; axe does not take an inline-block link for a link in a text block (it ends the check before comparing colours) | No template changes and every present and future cell of that shape is covered; looks the same (the link keeps its line, a long name wraps inside its own box); the underline stays under the pointer and on focus as decided | The reason sits in one comment of the stylesheet, not in each template |
| (b) Every second line a block (`.secondary` as `display: block`) | Cell text after the link starts a new block | Matches the layout of the data table | Covers only the elements that carry the class; a badge (inline flex) or a path in a cell still counts as text, so each new cell shape can fail again |
| (c) Underline links in cells | Reverses Q-UI-128 | Passes everywhere | The owner decided against it for tables and lists |

**Choice (links):** (a). A cell that holds a link and other things is not running text, the case Q-UI-128 kept the underline for.

How the language submenu is opened:

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A click on the trigger opens the submenu and never closes it (chosen) | The directive `troveOpenSubmenuOnClick` ([open-submenu-on-click.ts](../../web/src/app/shared/ui/open-submenu-on-click.ts)) swallows the click while the submenu is open and moves the focus into it; Escape and the left arrow still close it | Mouse, touch (the first tap opens) and keyboard (arrow right, Enter) all reach the languages as `menuitem`s of a `menu`, the ARIA menu pattern | One small directive over the CDK |
| (b) Languages as `menuitemradio` entries inside the user menu, no submenu | The theme menu's pattern; the current language is checked | No nested menu | R-UI-045 and the top bar's description are "Language with its submenu"; changes a decided structure for a bug in the hover/click interplay |

**Choice (submenu):** (a). The journey's roles (`menuitem` "Sprache", then `menuitem` "English") are what the ARIA menu pattern
gives a submenu; the test is right and stays unchanged.

**Rationale:** both findings came from the review's restyle and control swap, and both are found only in a real browser (jsdom
has no hover and no colours). Revisit (links) when axe changes what it counts as a text block, or when running text moves into
a table cell (then it needs the underline); revisit (submenu) when the CDK menu stops toggling an open trigger on click.

**Applied in the spec:** none; R-UI-044 and R-UI-045 already state the behaviour. Code: `.content :is(table, dl) a` in
[_shell.scss](../../web/src/styles/_shell.scss); `OpenSubmenuOnClick` and the `Language` item in
[app.html](../../web/src/app/app.html). Tests: `app.spec.ts` (the submenu stays open after hover and click); the browser
journeys `07-german-dark.spec.ts` and `vuln/15-vulnerabilities.spec.ts` (axe in both schemes).

### Q-UI-153 · The last Material controls become small shared pieces on the CDK and `@angular/aria`

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: Q-UI-126 moved the sign-in screens and the shell to trove's own controls and left the rest on Angular Material:
about 250 buttons in 80 files, 28 dialogs, 24 checkboxes, 5 tab groups with 10 tabs, 2 menus, one tooltip and the two
field components `TextField` and `SelectField` (a `mat-form-field` around a native control). Finishing it needed one
answer for how a screen opens a dialog, since the CDK's `Dialog` differs from `MatDialog` in its type parameters
(`open<Result, Data, Component>` against `open<Component, Data, Result>`), its result stream (`closed` against `afterClosed()`),
and in what it leaves to the caller (the dialog is named by nothing until a title is attached, and there is no close
directive in the CDK of this release).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A thin `TroveDialog` service on the CDK `Dialog`, with a title directive and a close directive (chosen) | One place sets `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal`, the first-tabbable focus, focus restore, the panel and backdrop classes and a width that never exceeds the window; `DialogTitle` names the container through the CDK's own `aria-labelledby` queue; `DialogClose` closes with an optional value | A dialog is opened and written the way the 22 call sites already were (component, data, result); the accessibility contract is in one tested file; no screen can forget the title association | One 90-line file of ours beside the CDK |
| (b) The CDK `Dialog` in each screen | `inject(Dialog)` and a config at every call site | Nothing of ours to maintain | The config (role, modal, focus, classes) repeated 22 times and the title association forgotten once; the reversed type parameters invite mistakes |
| (c) The native `<dialog>` element | `showModal()` | No library | The result and data plumbing, the focus return and the stacking with the CDK's overlays (menus, tooltips) are ours to write; jsdom lacks `showModal` |

**Choice (dialogs):** (a). The same decision for the rest:

- Buttons: `mat-flat-button` is `btn btn-confirm`, `mat-stroked-button` `btn btn-default`, `mat-button` `btn btn-tertiary`,
  `mat-icon-button` `btn btn-icon`: the shapes Q-UI-128 had already themed Material's variants to, so no screen changes its
  look by the move. A button that was `mat-flat-button` keeps being the confirm button even where it deletes; a destructive
  action asks through `Confirm` as before.
- Checkboxes: a small component `trove-checkbox`, not the bare input with a label in every template, because 24 uses share the
  label wrapper, the `describedBy` note and the `ariaLabel` of a row's box (the table's selection boxes have no visible label).
  The output is `checkedChange` with the new state, not `change`: a native `change` event bubbles from the input and would
  reach a `(change)` handler of the host with an `Event`.
- Tabs: a `trove-tab-group` over `@angular/aria`'s tabs (the roles, the arrow keys, Home and End, the roving tab stop) in the
  `.tab-nav` look of the package views, because the five groups switch a view in place and a tab that is a route is already
  a `.tab-nav` link. Only the selected tab's content is in the page, as with Material's tabs; content a screen wants created
  on selection is wrapped in `<ng-template troveTabContent>`.
- Tooltip: a directive on the CDK overlay with the hidden description of the CDK's `AriaDescriber`, so the help button of a
  table column is described whether or not the bubble shows (WCAG 1.4.13: Escape dismisses it, the pointer can move onto it).
- Menus: the CDK menu, as the user menu already was.
- Fields: the two field components render the label, the control and the text below with trove's classes; the label sits above
  and is bound with `for`, so every field has a visible, programmatic name (the `display: none` label of the density -2
  Material field that axe found in the browser tier cannot recur).
- Tokens: every `--mat-sys-*` property became a `--trove-*` property in `_tokens.scss`. The page palette moved over with its
  values; the error, inverse, banner and surface-container tones the screens read from Material's generated palette are
  literal `light-dark()` pairs with the values they had, so no screen changes its colour. Type scale properties became
  font shorthands (`--trove-type-*`), the corner sizes the radii (`--trove-radius-*`).
- Unit tests: `settle` follows each `whenStable` with a turn of the event loop through a message channel. With Material gone,
  nothing held the application unstable while a chain of awaits ran (the file tree's deep link loads one folder after the
  other), so six rounds no longer reached the end; a timer would not do, because specs with fake timers use `settle` too.

Rationale: every composite widget keeps its behaviour from the CDK or `@angular/aria` (focus trap and return, Escape,
roving focus, menu keys) and the screens carry no copy of it; the look is `_controls.scss` and `_dialog.scss`. The development
agent revisits the tabs if a screen needs a tab strip with overflow or closable tabs (the aria package has no pattern for
them), and the checkbox component if a form needs an indeterminate state.

**Applied in the spec:** Q-UI-126 (status), R-UI-001 (component library), R-UI-002 (density). Code: `web/src/app/shared/ui/`
(`dialog.ts`, `checkbox.ts`, `tabs.ts`, `tooltip.ts`), `web/src/styles/` (`_dialog.scss`, `_controls.scss`, `_tokens.scss`,
`main.scss`), `shared/access/fields.ts`, every screen that opened a `MatDialog` or used a Material control,
`web/package.json` and the lock file. Tests: `dialog.spec.ts`, `tabs.spec.ts`, `checkbox.spec.ts`, `tooltip.spec.ts`, and the
screens' specs, which query roles, labels and `[role="dialog"]`. Documented in
[design-language.md](../developer/design-language.md#controls) and [web-ui.md](../developer/web-ui.md#controls).

### Q-UI-163 · The URL is the project; what stays outside a project, and where the packages of a project come from

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: building [Q-UI-129](#q-ui-129--the-project-is-the-context-of-the-content-chosen-from-your-projects) needed four answers
it left open: how a screen learns its project, which content screens are not a project's, how the packages of one project are
listed, and what becomes of the administration an Owner had in the admin area.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The route is the project; instance-wide screens stay outside (chosen) | `/projects/:project/…` is a componentless parent, so every screen below it gets `project` as an input from the router; the shell reads the key from the same URL for the side bar, the switcher and the recent projects. Guides, client setup, profile and help stay outside a project; the advisory sources (an instance-wide setting) move to `/admin/advisory-sources`; the packages list asks the server for `project=`; an Owner manages the project inside it and has no admin area | One source of truth that is also the bookmark; a screen cannot disagree with the address; no stored choice to go stale; the admin area is only for system capabilities | Every link to content names the project; a link from a place that knows only a repository (audit, endpoint rules, client setup) derives it from the qualified name |
| (b) The project in a global store, the URL as before | A selected project in a service or a preference filters the content screens | No route changes | The state R-UI-041 had and Q-UI-129 rejected: the address does not say where you are |
| (c) Everything under the project, guides and advisory sources too | The guides get the project, and the sources screen would need a project it does not have | One rule | The sources are the installation's, not a project's; the guides of a format or a class are not either, and the client setup page already takes a repository of any project |

**Choice:** (a), with these consequences, each decided here:

- **The key comes from the URL as soon as the router has recognised it.** `ProjectContext` follows `RoutesRecognized`, not
  `NavigationEnd`, so a screen that asks for the project in its constructor (the remembered package views of
  `PackageMemory`) gets the new one; a navigation that is cancelled or fails puts the old URL back. A key that names no project
  the caller sees (a user who reads one repository through a policy) is still the context: the screen shows what the API
  answers.
- **The projects of the caller** are `GET /api/v1/projects`; the recently visited keys (five) are kept per signed-in principal
  in browser storage (R-UI-043, R-UI-046), a convenience only. With exactly one project the start route redirects into it.
- **The packages of a project** are `GET /api/v1/packages?project=<key>`: the filter is the physical repositories of the project,
  intersected with `repository=`, in the view service (`Topology.InProject`) so the visibility rules of R-API-029 apply
  unchanged. The package page itself (`/projects/:project/packages/:format/:name…`) is the package across the repositories the
  caller may read, as the lookup returns it; its repositories tab names the project of each repository.
- **The vulnerability report** is the project's (`project=` of the findings, summary and trend); the advisory page lists the
  findings of the advisory the caller may read in any project, each linking to its finding in that finding's project. The
  instance-wide search is [Q-UI-130](#q-ui-130--the-auditor-has-an-instance-wide-vulnerability-dashboard-in-the-admin-area).
- **The Owner's administration moves into the project** (members, policies, service accounts, CI identity, settings), so the
  admin area is shown to a caller with a capability only and `isProjectOwner` is gone from the session store.
- **A project's setup of a page that serves both** (the repository list and wizard, the policy list) is one component that reads
  whether the route carries `:project`; the admin area's list is the same component without it, with the project as a column
  and a filter.

Rationale: the address and the side bar then say where you are, which is what the owner asked for. The development agent
revisits the package page if a project needs its own view of a package (versions only of its repositories), which needs the
versions API to take `project=` as well, and the guides if they gain a notion of "the repositories of this project".

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-002, R-UI-003, R-UI-020, R-UI-021, R-UI-041 and the preference note of R-API-021; the gap H-550 is
closed and its block removed; [vulnerability-scanning.md](vulnerability-scanning.md) R-VULN-022 (the routes). `GET /api/v1/packages`
gained `project` (`api/openapi.yaml`, `internal/api/v1/packages_api.go`, `internal/packages/view/topology.go`; tests
`TestR_API_029_ProjectNarrowsToThePhysicalRepositoriesOfTheProject`, `TestR_API_029_FilterParsing`).

### Q-UI-165 · The security dashboard is the content report mounted in the admin area, with its own links, project column and search

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: [Q-UI-130](#q-ui-130--the-auditor-has-an-instance-wide-vulnerability-dashboard-in-the-admin-area) asks for counts, a
trend, a search by advisory, package and project, a list with the project as a column and the triage of each finding in the
admin area. The Vulnerabilities screen of a project (`/projects/:project/vulnerabilities`, Q-UI-163) already has the counts, the trend (`--trove-chart-*`), the list with
its filters, the bulk triage, and the finding and advisory screens behind it; only the `project` filter and the search
were missing in the UI for the whole instance.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The same screens, mounted a second time below `/admin/security` (chosen) | The report, the finding and the advisory screens are routed in the project and below `/admin/security`; a route-level provider (`VULN_CONTEXT`) says whether a screen reads every project (`instanceWide`), which switches on the project column, the search and the heading, and `vulnCommands` builds every link to a sibling screen inside the place the screen was opened in (the advisory sources are the installation's single page `/admin/advisory-sources`, Q-UI-163) | One implementation of the counts, the trend, the filters, the triage and the export; the project's own screen and the dashboard cannot drift apart; the `project` input of the report is the route parameter in a project and the query parameter in the dashboard | A change to the report is a change to both screens; the report component carries two small conditions |
| (b) A second report component for the dashboard | A copy with the project column and the search | The project screen stays untouched | Two lists, two sets of filters and chips and two triage flows to keep equal; a fix lands in one of them |
| (c) The project filter and a project column on the content screen, no admin screen | One screen for both | No new route | Q-UI-130 (b), which the owner rejected: it mixes the project context with the instance |

**Choice:** (a). The entry *Security* of the admin area is shown to a holder of `vulnerabilities:triage` or
`content:metadata-read` (`NavItem.anyCapability`); the admin area's start page is the dashboard for a caller who holds one of
the two and none of `settings:read`, `repositories:read-config` and `projects:read`. A holder of
`content:metadata-read` alone reads; the selection column, the bulk action and the status buttons of the finding appear only
with `vulnerabilities:triage` (R-UI-005), as in a project, and the dashboard says so. The advisory field of the search
writes the identifier in its canonical spelling (`cve-2021-23337` becomes `CVE-2021-23337`, a GHSA identifier keeps its
lower-case groups), because the API compares identifiers exactly and finds a finding by any alias of its advisory (R-VULN-006).
The package field is a prefix search (`packagePrefix`), the project field a project key (`project`); the exact package name,
the version and every other filter stay in the filter panel.

**Rationale:** the dashboard is the report with a wider scope, and the API already scopes by `project`; what differs is where
the links go and which columns show. The development agent would revisit this when the dashboard needs a layout of its own
(per-project tiles, a ranking of packages) that the report's header cannot grow into, or when the project's Vulnerabilities
screen needs more than `VULN_CONTEXT` to tell the two apart; then the dashboard becomes its own component over the same
services.

**Applied in the spec:** Q-UI-130 (status: built), R-VULN-022 (instance-wide bullet), H-551 closed. Code:
`web/src/app/features/vulnerabilities/` (`vuln-context.ts`, `security.routes.ts`, `vulnerability-report.ts` and `.html`),
`web/src/app/core/navigation.ts`, `auth-guard.ts`, `help-topics.ts`, `web/src/app/app.routes.ts`. Tests: `security-dashboard.spec.ts`,
`admin-home.spec.ts`, `vulnerabilities-api.spec.ts`; the browser journey `web/e2e/vuln/16-security-dashboard.spec.ts` (axe in both
schemes). Documented in [web-ui.md](../developer/web-ui.md) and [vulnerabilities.md](../developer/vulnerabilities.md).

### Q-UI-166 · The avatar is seeded with the ID of the principal

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the owner's decision of 2026-11-07 (R-UI-002) gives every user without an uploaded avatar a generated robot that is
the same everywhere. The seed decides the robot.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) `principal.id` of `GET /api/v1/whoami` (chosen) | The UUID of the principal | Stable for the life of the account, so a rename changes nothing; not an address; already in the response the UI loads; the same on every replica and in every session | Not human-readable, which does not matter for an image |
| (b) `principal.name` | The user name | Readable | A rename (an IdP that changes a username) changes the robot; two principal kinds can share a name |
| (c) The e-mail address | The address of the identity provider | Stable at some IdPs | Personal data in a place that does not need it, and not every principal has one |
| (d) The token or session ID | Per credential | None | Changes with every sign-in: the robot would not be the same |

**Choice:** (a).
**Rationale:** the ID is the identifier trove itself keys the principal by; it is not a secret (it is in the API response and
the audit log). The development agent would revisit this when the user has an uploaded avatar (the image then wins) or when
another principal kind needs a different identity.
**Applied:** R-UI-002. Code: `web/src/app/app.html` (`[seed]="session.whoami()?.principal?.id"`), `web/src/app/shared/ui/avatar.ts`.

### Q-UI-167 · The robot is rendered in the browser from the bundled Bottts style and loaded as a lazy chunk

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the owner (R-UI-002) wants DiceBear's Bottts avatars with nothing requested from outside at runtime; everything of
DiceBear is to be in the web container. The UI's CSP admits `img-src 'self' data:` (`internal/webui/csp.go`).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) `@dicebear/core` and the style definition of `@dicebear/styles`, rendered in the browser, shown as a data URI in an `<img>`, in a lazy chunk (chosen) | `new Avatar(new Style(bottts.json), {seed, size, idRandomization: false}).toDataUri()` in `shared/ui/robot.ts`, imported dynamically by the avatar component | Nothing leaves the origin; the CSP stays as it is (no `innerHTML`, no `bypassSecurityTrust*`); the chunk (246 kB, 43 kB compressed) is not in the initial bundle, which stays at 588 kB | The robot appears a moment after the shell; an `<img>` of a data URI cannot take the theme's colours |
| (b) The same, in the initial bundle | A static import | No flash | The initial bundle grows by 247 kB (to 835 kB), over the 800 kB warning of `angular.json`, for a 32 px image |
| (c) The robots pre-rendered at build time | A set of SVG files | No library in the browser | A user is one of unboundedly many; a seed has no finite set of images |
| (d) DiceBear's HTTP API or a CDN | `<img src="https://api.dicebear.com/…">` | No dependency | Forbidden by the owner; a request to a third party for every page load; the CSP would need the host |
| (e) The server renders the SVG | A Go endpoint | No library in the browser | The DiceBear library is JavaScript; a second implementation of its generator would have to be kept equal to it |

The style comes from `@dicebear/styles` (version 10 of DiceBear moved the styles out of per-style packages into definition
files; `@dicebear/bottts` ends at 9.4.3 and needs core 9). Core 10.7.0 and styles 10.6.0 are the newest stable releases (both
published 2026-08-26); `@dicebear/styles` has a version line of its own, so the two pins differ. Only `bottts.json` is imported, so the bundler
takes that one definition (92 kB) and not the other styles of the package. Renovate's weekly group of non-major updates
carries both; a major goes through the Dependency Dashboard approval (`renovate.json`).

Licences (read in the installed packages): DiceBear's code, `@dicebear/core`, MIT (Florian Körner). The Bottts artwork is by
Pablo Stanley, licence "Free for personal and commercial use" (https://bottts.com/), repeated in the `meta` block of the
definition and in the metadata of every SVG the library renders; it permits this use. It asks for no attribution beyond the
text kept in the SVG's metadata, and trove keeps it there. `@dicebear/styles` ships the licences of all its styles in
`LICENSE.md`; Angular copies that file into `3rdpartylicenses.txt`, which every installation serves at
`/ui/<locale>/3rdpartylicenses.txt` (Q-UI-144), so the notice of the Bottts artwork travels with the bundle. The notice also
lists the licences of the styles that are not bundled (some are CC BY 4.0); they are not used. `web/scripts/build-embed.mjs`
fails the build when the notice lacks `@dicebear/core`, `@dicebear/styles`, the Bottts entry or its licence text, and when a script
of the bundle names `api.dicebear.com`.

**Choice:** (a).
**Rationale:** it is the only option that satisfies the owner's constraint without a second generator, and the lazy chunk keeps
the initial budget (R-UI-001) where it was. The development agent would revisit this when the avatar is shown on enough
screens that the flash matters, or when DiceBear's licensing of the Bottts artwork changes (the notice check would show it).
**Applied:** R-UI-002, R-UI-001 (third-party notices). Code: `web/package.json` (exact pins), `web/src/app/shared/ui/robot.ts`,
`avatar.ts`, `web/scripts/build-embed.mjs`. Tests: `avatar.spec.ts` (same seed same SVG, other seed other SVG, no external reference in the SVG,
an uploaded URL wins), `app.spec.ts` (the top bar), `web/e2e/tests/01-sign-in.spec.ts` (no request leaves the origin).

### Q-UI-168 · The robot keeps the badge the letter had, on the theme's surface fill

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the letter badge was a 32 px circle on the accent fill; the owner's rule is the reference's look without unasked
styling, so the avatar keeps the 32 px circle and the hover (`brightness(1.1)`).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A transparent SVG on `--trove-surface-variant` of the host (chosen) | `#ececef` in the light scheme, `#3a383f` in the dark one, round | Follows the chosen theme, including the explicit choice of R-API-021, which a data URI cannot; no new colour | The robot's dark parts sit on a dark fill in the dark scheme (the head is the robot's own colour and fills most of the circle) |
| (b) A fixed background colour in the SVG (`backgroundColor`) | One colour for both schemes | The image is self-contained | A colour outside the palette; wrong in one of the schemes |
| (c) The accent fill as before | `--trove-accent-fill` | Unchanged look | The accent is for actions; a robot on it looks like a button state |

**Choice:** (a). The SVG is rendered at 64 px for sharpness at 2x and shown at 32 px (`inline-size: 2rem`); the options are
only `seed`, `size` and `idRandomization: false` (the ids inside the SVG are not randomised, so the output is a function of the
seed).
**Rationale:** the least styling that works in both schemes. The development agent would revisit this when the owner
wants a coloured background per user (`backgroundColor` in the options).
**Applied:** R-UI-002. Code: `web/src/styles/_shell.scss` (`.avatar`), `web/src/app/shared/ui/avatar.ts`.

### Q-API-204 · The backup endpoints use `settings:read`, list `summary` as a reserved name and declare their state fields as strings

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Follow the table of R-API-050 literally | The permission is `system.read`; `summary` needs no reservation; `state`, `operation` and `trigger` are enums | Matches the text | `system.read` is the name of the capability `settings:read` (R-OPS page); the route check of R-API-004 lists every literal sibling of a `{key}` segment; the code generator renames the existing `ReplicaState` constants when a second enum has the values `failed` or `completed`, which would change the code of every other page |
| (b) `settings:read`, `summary` in `x-trove-reserved-names`, strings with the values in the description (chosen) | The operations declare `permission: settings:read`; `BackupRunId` lists `summary`; the schema types are strings | No other page's generated names change; the check passes; the authorization step needs no new permission | The generated client does not type the state; the UI compares strings |

**Choice:** (b).

**Rationale:** The three choices follow from the existing code: the declared permission names, the reserved-name test and the generator's collision rule. A UUID never equals `summary`, so the reservation costs nothing. The development agent would revisit the string types when the generator keeps enum constants per type.

**Applied:** R-API-050 table and permission column; `api/openapi.yaml` (M5 backup); `internal/api/v1/backups_api.go`.

### Q-API-207 · An avatar is read at a path named by its digest

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the owner decided that a user can upload an avatar and that the `api` role serves it from trove's origin (R-API-055). The UI shows another user's avatar in lists, in members and in audit rows, so a read path must work for any user, and the user record has to tell the UI whether a user has an avatar or the generated one applies.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) `GET /api/v1/avatars/{digest}`, the SHA-256 of the stored image; the user record carries the path (chosen) | The URL names the content; a replacement is a new URL | The answer can be cached forever (`immutable`) and the browser never asks again; no username in the URL, so a rename breaks nothing; a lookup by digest cannot be confused with any other user's data | The record has to carry the URL; the old URL is `404` after a replacement, so a page that was rendered before the change shows a broken image until it reloads |
| (b) `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/avatar` | One stable URL per user | The UI can build the URL from the name | The URL is stable but the content is not: a cache needs revalidation on every use or a query string; a rename moves the URL; the UI still needs to know whether the user has one (a `404` per list row otherwise) |
| (c) The image inline in the user record as a data URL | No second request | No new route | Every user list carries up to 100 images of tens of KiB, uncacheable; the JSON answers are `no-store` (R-API-017) |
| (d) A configured URL per user from the identity provider (`picture` claim) | trove shows an external image | No upload, no storage | The owner decided on upload; a foreign origin in `img-src` and a third party that sees every page view (R-UI-001 loads nothing from outside) |

**Choice:** (a). `PUT /api/v1/users/me/avatar` and `DELETE /api/v1/users/me/avatar` write, `DELETE /api/v1/users/{username}/avatar` is the moderation, `GET /api/v1/avatars/{digest}` reads. The route answers only for a digest that a user's avatar currently names (`AvatarByDigest`), so it is no way to read another blob of the store.

**Rationale:** the content address turns the two hard parts of serving an image, caching and consistency, into properties of the URL. The cost is a dangling URL in a page that was rendered before a replacement; the UI re-reads the user record after its own upload, and another user's replacement reaches it with the next read of that record. Revisit when the avatar gets sizes (a 32 px and a 96 px rendition): then the digest stays and a `size` query parameter or a second digest is added.

**Applied:** R-API-055; `api/openapi.yaml` (`setAvatar`, `removeAvatar`, `removeUserAvatar`, `getAvatar`, `User.avatarUrl`); `internal/api/v1/avatar_api.go`; `internal/meta/postgres/queries/avatars.sql`.

### Q-API-208 · An upload is decoded, bounded and re-encoded as a 256 pixel PNG

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the owner fixed PNG, JPEG and WebP only, never SVG, re-encoded on the server, at most 1 MiB. The body is untrusted: a decoder reads attacker-chosen bytes, a header can declare a size that costs gigabytes, and an image carries metadata (a camera's GPS position) and can carry a payload after its end. Open were the bound on the size in pixels, the output, the animated case, the metadata and the cost bound.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Sniff the content, read the size from the header and bound it, decode, crop to the centre square, scale to 256 x 256, encode a new PNG; animation is refused (chosen) | `internal/avatar.Process`; at most 4,194,304 pixels (2048 x 2048) and at least 32 x 32; two decodes at a time per replica | Nothing of the upload survives but its pixels; the size is refused before an allocation; one fixed output, so the UI needs no variants and the digest is stable; memory is bounded by an estimate from the header, 48 MiB a decode and 96 MiB a replica (Q-API-211) | A 12 Mpixel photo under 1 MiB (rare, heavy compression) is refused and the user resizes it; 16-bit PNGs are reduced to 8 bits |
| (b) Re-encode in the original format at the original size | Strip the metadata and keep the image | No scaling | A 1 MiB JPEG is served to a 32 px slot; the format and size vary; a stored JPEG is still a parser's input in the browser |
| (c) Take the first frame of an animation | Decode as the decoders do | More uploads succeed | The decoders differ (the PNG decoder silently reads the default image, the WebP decoder refuses); a user who uploads an animation expects it to move, so a still is a surprise; refusal says so |
| (d) A larger pixel bound (16 Mpixel) | Phone photos work | Fewer refusals | 128 MiB per decode at the widest pixel, 256 MiB for two (more for a progressive JPEG); the replica's request memory is charged at 640 KiB (Q-ARCH-328), so the decode must bound itself |
| (e) Decode in a separate process | An isolated image worker | A decoder bug cannot reach the API process | A second binary role and a pipe for a feature of 32 px images; the decoders are the Go standard library's and `golang.org/x/image`'s, which are memory safe. Not done: H-560 |

**Choice:** (a). The numbers are constants of the product (`avatar.MaxUpload` 1 MiB, `OutputSide` 256, `MinSide` 32, `MaxPixels` 4,194,304, `MaxDecodeBytes` 48 MiB, `MaxScans` 64, `DecodeTimeout` 5 s, `MaxConcurrent` 2, `BusyWait` 2 s), not configuration; the first version of this decision bounded the memory by the pixels alone and was corrected by Q-API-211: an operator should not be able to widen the input of an image decoder. 256 pixels is twice the larger of the two sizes the UI shows (32 and 96 px) at a display density of two. The Catmull-Rom filter of `golang.org/x/image/draw` scales; the centre square is the crop. Transparency is kept. The EXIF orientation of a JPEG is read from the first Exif segment, bounds-checked in the segment, and applied to the scaled square (the centre square of a turned image is the turned centre square of the stored one, so the turn costs 65,536 pixels, not the source). A panic of a decoder is caught and is an undecodable image. The request memory guard (Q-ARCH-328) charges a request the bytes of a download; it does not know the decode, so the processor bounds it itself (a slot per decode, waiting 2 s, `503 server_busy` with `Retry-After: 1`); the 1 MiB body is held in addition. `golang.org/x/image` is added to `go.mod` once, at the latest release, and only its `webp` decoder and `draw` are imported.

**Rationale:** the safest handling of an image is to keep nothing of it but the pixels; everything the owner asked for (re-encode, only three formats, 1 MiB) follows from that, and the pixel bound is what turns a decompression bomb into a `422` before it costs anything. The development agent revisits the pixel bound when users report refusals of ordinary photos: the cost is linear, and 3 Mpixel more per slot is 24 MiB. It revisits the refusal of animations if the owner wants an animated avatar.

**Applied:** R-API-055; `internal/avatar/process.go`, `internal/avatar/orient.go`; `go.mod` (`golang.org/x/image`). Tests: `TestR_API_055_*` in `internal/avatar/process_test.go`.

### Q-API-209 · The image answer has its own headers and an immutable private cache

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: R-API-017 gives every `/api/v1/` answer `Cache-Control: no-store` and a CSP of `default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`; the avatar is a picture shown many times on a page and in every list.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) `private, max-age=31536000, immutable`, a strong ETag that is the digest, and the content headers of an image (chosen) | The browser keeps the picture for a year and does not revalidate; a shared cache does not keep it | One request per avatar per browser; a list of 100 rows costs nothing after the first | The picture stays in the browser of a user who was signed out; it is a 256 px avatar, and the digest is unguessable |
| (b) `no-store` like the JSON answers | Every row of every list asks again | Nothing to reason about | 100 requests per page, each a database lookup and an object-store read |
| (c) `private, no-cache` with the ETag | Revalidate each time | Always current | Still a request and a lookup per row; the URL changes with the content, so there is nothing to be current about |
| (d) `public` | A proxy may keep it | Fewer reads | The answer needs a credential; a shared cache would hand it to callers without one |

**Choice:** (a). The headers are `Content-Type: image/png`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; sandbox`, `Content-Disposition: inline; filename="avatar.png"` and `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin`. `If-None-Match` answers `304`. The bytes are read through the verifying path of the blob store and compared with the digest once more before they are sent, as for the shared UI assets (Q-UI-143).

**Rationale:** the stored bytes are trove's own PNG, but the response is still defended as if it were not: nosniff and the sandboxing CSP keep a browser that is pointed at the URL from reading it as anything else, and `Content-Disposition: inline` with a fixed name keeps the name out of the answer. A removed avatar is `404` for any new request, and a browser that already has it keeps it until its cache entry ends (H-561). The development agent revisits `immutable` if avatars are ever removed for legal reasons that a browser's copy must not outlive.

**Applied:** R-API-055 (the image answer); `internal/api/v1/avatar_api.go` (`GetAvatar`).

### Q-API-210 · The user record carries avatarUrl and its ETag follows the avatar

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the UI reads the avatar of a user from the user record. The record has a strong ETag, the revision of the principal (R-API-012), and `GET /api/v1/users/{username}` answers `304` for it; a change of a member that the record shows must change the tag, or a client keeps the old URL (R-API-012, "a representation that carries a member which changes without a new revision has a tag that follows the member").

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The avatar row bumps `principal.revision`, as the identity links do (chosen) | A trigger on `user_avatars` calls `principal_revision_bump('user_id')` on insert, delete and a change of the blob | No writer can forget it; the tag is the revision as for every other member; one rule | An administrator who loaded the user, then sees the user change the avatar, gets `412` on the `PATCH` and reloads |
| (b) A view part in the tag, `"<revision>-<digest8>"` | The tag follows the digest without touching the revision | No `412` for the administrator | `If-Match` of the `PATCH` compares the revision (`Precondition.Revision(view)`), so the view has to be threaded through the user handlers; two ways to tag one resource |
| (c) `avatarUrl` outside the record, a call of its own | The UI asks `GET /users/{u}/avatar-info` | The record is untouched | A request per row of a list |

**Choice:** (a). The trigger fires only when the blob changes, so the upload of the image a user already has leaves the revision and the record alone. `avatarUrl` is read-only: `PATCH /api/v1/users/{username}` accepts and ignores it (R-API-013). `toUser` fills it from `principal.User.AvatarSHA256`, which the manager reads for a batch of users in one statement (`AvatarDigests`), so a list of 500 users costs one query more, not 500.

**Rationale:** the avatar is part of the representation, so the tag has to follow it, and (b) costs a second tagging scheme; a user changes the avatar a few times in a lifetime and an administrator edits profile data rarely, so the race of (a) is real and cheap to repair. A user who alternates two pictures on purpose can keep an administrator's conditional edit failing, which is recorded as H-562 and not closed: the remedy is a read and a retry, or `If-Match: *`. Revisit when administrators meet the `412` in practice.

**Applied:** R-API-055, R-AUTH-016 (the record); migration `user_avatars` (the triggers `user_avatars_revision_change` and `user_avatars_revision_replace`); `internal/auth/principal/manager.go` (`fillAvatars`), `internal/api/v1/users_api.go` (`toUser`). Test: `TestR_API_055_AvatarLifecycle`.

### Q-UI-169 · The shell reads the avatar of the signed-in user from the user record, in a store of its own

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: R-UI-051 wants the top bar to change after an upload without a reload. `whoami` (the session) does not carry
`avatarUrl`, which is on the user record (R-API-055).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) An `AvatarStore` (`core/avatar-store.ts`): reads `GET /api/v1/users/me` once per signed-in principal, the profile sets it after a change (chosen) | One signal, `url`, which the top bar's avatar takes as `imageUrl` | No change to `whoami` or the session store, whose specs stay as they are; the top bar and the profile share one value; a failed read leaves the robot | One more request after the sign-in |
| (b) `avatarUrl` on `whoami` | The session answer names it | No extra request | A change of the API after R-API-055 was built and tested; `whoami` is also the answer for service accounts |
| (c) The top bar reads the record on every navigation | No store | Always current | A request per navigation for a value that changes when this tab changes it |

**Choice:** (a). A service account and a CI token get no read (`available`), because they have no avatar and the two `me` routes answer
`403` for them. Another browser tab of the same user shows the change at its next load; the avatar is a convenience, not a
permission.
**Rationale:** the shell needs one value, and the tab that changes it is the tab that shows it. The development agent would revisit this
when the avatar is shown on lists (the list items carry their own `avatarUrl`) or when `whoami` is extended for other reasons.
**Applied:** R-UI-051. Code: `web/src/app/core/avatar-store.ts`, `app.ts`, `app.html`, `features/profile/profile.ts`.

### Q-UI-170 · The profile card sends the chosen file at once, and "Remove avatar" asks first

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the reference's "Public avatar" lets the user choose a file and saves it with the form's "Update profile settings"; the
profile of trove has no such form for identity (name and email come from the identity provider, R-UI-029), only the preferences.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The file is sent when chosen; the card shows the result (chosen) | **Choose file…** opens the picker, the answer replaces the image | One step; the card does not mix with the preferences' save button, which would save two unrelated things; a refusal appears where the file was chosen | No preview before the change; replacing is one click after the picker |
| (b) Choose, preview, then a **Save avatar** button | The reference's two steps | A preview before anything is stored | A pending state to keep (a chosen file, a preview URL to revoke) for a 256 pixel image the server re-encodes anyway |
| (c) The preview inside the preferences form | One save for everything | Fewer buttons | The preferences are saved with `If-Match` and a conflict dialog; the image has neither |

**Choice:** (a). **Remove avatar** opens the confirmation dialog of the other destructive actions (the reference confirms too), because the

**Rationale:** the image is its own resource with its own endpoint (R-API-055), so the card is its own unit. The development agent would
revisit this when the owner wants the crop dialog of the reference.
