### Q-UI-171 · The browser checks type, size and pixel size, and leaves the animation check to the server

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the owner asked to mirror what is cheap in the browser; the server decides the format from the bytes and finds an
animated PNG or WebP only by reading the file (R-API-055).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Not empty, the declared type, the 1 MiB limit and the pixel size by `createImageBitmap`; no animation check (chosen) | `features/profile/avatar-file.ts`; the refusals use the server's codes, so one sentence serves both | No request for the common mistakes (a screenshot as GIF, a camera photo of 20 MB); a few lines; the sizer is an injection token, so tests need no real decoder | An animated WebP costs one upload before it is refused; a browser that cannot decode a WebP refuses it as unreadable |
| (b) Also parse the headers for animation (APNG `acTL`, WebP `ANIM`) | A second parser in the browser | Saves the one request | Another parser to keep equal to the server's, for a case the server handles in milliseconds |
| (c) No checks, the server decides | Every file is sent | Nothing to keep equal | Up to 1 MiB, or a file of any size read by the browser, goes out for a refusal the browser knows in advance |

**Choice:** (a). The 1 MiB limit is checked before decoding, so a huge file is never read into a bitmap; the declared type is the browser's
guess from the file name, and the server checks the bytes against it anyway.
**Rationale:** the browser's checks are a courtesy; the server's are the control, and nothing here relaxes them. The development agent would
revisit this when users report animated images as a common mistake.
**Applied:** R-UI-051. Code: `web/src/app/features/profile/avatar-file.ts`, `avatar-messages.ts`. Tests: `profile-avatar.spec.ts`;
the browser journey `web/e2e/tests/15-avatar.spec.ts`.

### Q-API-205 · The backup block of the system information uses `expectedIntervalSeconds` and has nullable members

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) `expectedInterval` as a duration string such as `"24h"` | The form that R-API-050 named | One form with the configuration | R-API-003 puts the unit into the name of a duration, and R-OPS-004's example and the summary already use `expectedIntervalSeconds`; two spellings for one value |
| (b) `expectedIntervalSeconds` (chosen) | The same name and unit as the summary and the gauge | One spelling; a script reads both answers the same way | The configuration key is a duration string |

**Choice:** (b). The block is an object with the members `expectedIntervalSeconds`, `lastSuccessAt`, `overdue` and `lastRunState` (the state of the newest run of any operation, `null` before one exists). The block itself is `null` on a replica that does not read the runs and when the table cannot be read: the other database facts of the answer are best effort too, and a failing read of this block must not take the diagnostic answer down.

**Rationale:** R-OPS-004 and R-API-050 disagreed; the unit-in-the-name rule decides it. The development agent would revisit the `null` block if a client needs to tell "unreadable" from "not wired".

**Applied:** R-API-050 and R-OPS-004 text; `api/openapi.yaml` (`BackupInfo`, `SystemInfo.backup`); `internal/api/v1/backups_api.go` (`backupInfo`).

### Q-API-206 · A run's `leaseExpired` and the overdue mark are judged on the database's clock

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The replica's clock | `time.Now()` | No extra read | The lease is written relative to the database's `now()` (R-BAK-010); a replica whose clock is a minute off would disagree with the backup pod, the next run and the gauges |
| (b) The database's clock (chosen) | `RunReader.ActiveRuns` returns it; a list or a single run reads it only when a run of the answer is in an active state | Every replica, the gauge and the abandon rule judge a lease at the same instant | One more read when an active run is in the answer |

**Choice:** (b).

**Rationale:** The lease is the database's decision (Q-BAK-4); the API only reports it. At most one create or delete run is active, so the extra read is bounded. The development agent would revisit this if a verify storm makes active runs common in lists.

**Applied:** R-API-050 (`leaseExpired`, `overdue`); `internal/api/v1/backups_api.go`.

### Q-API-211 · The work and the memory of a decode are bounded from the header, and a decode has a deadline

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: a security audit of Q-API-208 found that it bounded the pixels but not what a decoder does with them. The standard JPEG decoder walks every block once per scan, so a progressive 2048 x 2048 file with about 65,000 one-block scans, which fits in 1 MiB, takes minutes of CPU, holds one of the two decode slots, ignores that the client left and passes the 30 s of R-API-017. A progressive or four-component JPEG also holds more per pixel than the 8 bytes the decision counted (four bytes of coefficients for every component of every pixel: about 96 MiB for a CMYK image of 2048 x 2048), and the scaler adds a buffer of 256 x side x 32 bytes (16 MiB), so a slot could hold about 110 MiB, a replica 220 MiB, which the memory guard does not see.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Walk the JPEG markers before the slot and refuse more than 64 scans; estimate the memory of a decode from the header and refuse above 48 MiB; give every decode a 5 s deadline through the reader (chosen) | `walkJPEG`, `decodeCost`, `ctxReader` in `internal/avatar/process.go`; the new `422` code `too_complex` | The bomb is refused in microseconds without a slot; the deadline ends any long decode of any format at its next read, and a client that left stops the work; the bound on memory is a number the tests pin | A 1,600 x 1,600 progressive photo is accepted but a 2048 x 2048 one is not; the estimate is a table of bytes per pixel that has to follow the decoders |
| (b) Only the deadline | A reader that fails after 5 s | Little code | Each such upload still burns 5 s of a slot, and two uploads at a time starve the others of slots; the memory stays unbounded by the header |
| (c) Charge the estimate to the admission guard | `SettleMemory` with the estimate | One accounting for memory | `Ticket.Settle` caps one reader at the admission charge (640 KiB), so it cannot charge 48 MiB; a charge at the door needs a guard change (H-563) |
| (d) A smaller pixel bound for everything | 1 Mpixel | One number | Refuses ordinary 1600 x 1200 photos to protect against a rare class |
| (e) Scale in two steps | A cheap first pass | A smaller scaler buffer | The decoded image, not the scaler, is the larger part; more code on untrusted pixels |

**Choice:** (a). `MaxScans` is 64 (encoders write about ten), `DecodeTimeout` 5 s, `MaxDecodeBytes` 48 MiB, so two slots hold 96 MiB at the worst. The estimate is 4 bytes a pixel for an 8-bit PNG, 8 for a 16-bit PNG or a WebP, the number of components for a baseline JPEG, five times that for a progressive one, plus 256 x short side x 32 bytes. A decode that exceeds its deadline and a file with too many scans answer `422` with `errors[0].code` `too_complex`; a decode above the memory bound answers `422` `invalid_dimensions`, whose text says that a progressive JPEG, a four-component JPEG or a 16-bit PNG may have fewer pixels. The UI has the sentence for `too_complex` in both locales.

**Rationale:** the cheapest defence against a decompression bomb is to refuse what the header already shows; the deadline is the defence for what it does not. The bound of 96 MiB is still invisible to the admission guard and is recorded as H-563. The development agent revisits the numbers when users report refusals of ordinary photos, and the charge when the guard can take an estimate at the door.

**Applied:** R-API-055; [user-avatars.md](../security/user-avatars.md) (steps 5 to 8, H-563); `internal/avatar/process.go`; UI: `web/src/app/features/profile/avatar-messages.ts`, `web/src/locale/messages.xlf`, `messages.de.xlf`. Tests: `TestR_API_055_RefusesAJPEGWithManyScans`, `TestR_API_055_StopsADecodeAtItsDeadline`, `TestR_API_055_BoundsTheMemoryOfADecodeFromTheHeader`.

### Q-API-212 · A conditional read of an avatar is answered from the lookup, with the cache policy of the image

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: `GET /api/v1/avatars/{digest}` opened the blob (a database lookup and a verified object-store read) before it compared `If-None-Match`, and the shared `NotModified` puts `Cache-Control: no-store` on the 304, which by RFC 9111 section 4.3.4 replaces the `immutable` policy of the stored entry.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Look the digest up first; on a match answer 304 with the image's `Cache-Control` and the ETag, without opening the blob; open only for a 200 (chosen) | `AvatarService.Has`, `IfNoneMatchHits` | A revalidation costs one row; the browser keeps its policy | Two lookups for a 200 (the lookup of `Has` and the one of `Open`) |
| (b) Keep the order, fix the header | Only the 304 header changes | Smaller change | Every revalidation still reads the object store |
| (c) Answer 304 for any digest that matches, without a lookup | No database | Cheapest | A removed avatar would be revalidated as current, and the route would confirm digests it does not serve |

**Choice:** (a). A digest that no avatar names is `404` also when the tag matches.

**Rationale:** the 304 is the common answer for an immutable resource; it should not cost an object-store read and must not weaken what the browser stored. The second lookup of a 200 is one primary-key read. Revisit when the lookup becomes a measurable cost of list pages.

**Applied:** R-API-055; `internal/api/v1/avatar_api.go` (`GetAvatar`), `internal/api/v1/etag.go` (`IfNoneMatchHits`), `internal/avatar/store.go` (`Has`). Tests: `TestR_API_055_AConditionalReadAnswers304WithTheImagesCachePolicyAndWithoutReadingTheBlob`, `TestR_API_055_AvatarLifecycle`.

### Q-API-213 · A token limited to part of its owner's rights does not change the owner's avatar

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the two `me` routes declared `authenticated: true` and the handler checked only that the principal is a user, so a token made for one repository or one capability (R-AUTH-024: the scope is a ceiling on the owner's rights) could change the owner's profile picture, a right the scope never names.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A token must inherit the owner's rights (`scope.Inherit`); a session always may (chosen) | `avatarOwner` answers `403` for a token with a narrower scope | A token made for one task cannot do an unrelated thing as its owner; a script with a full personal token still can | A restricted token can never set an avatar, though the avatar is harmless |
| (b) Only a session | Tokens refused | The strictest | A script cannot provision its owner's avatar; the API would have a browser-only write |
| (c) Leave it | Any token of a user | No code | The scope is a ceiling only where a handler remembers to apply it |

**Choice:** (a). The administrator's removal of another user's avatar is a permission route and follows the token scope through the decision point as every `identities:write` operation does.

**Rationale:** the scope is the owner's promise that a token does only what it was made for; an `authenticated` route that changes the owner's data has to keep it. The same pattern existed on the routes of the UI preferences and of the own sessions; Q-API-214 lifts this check into a route attribute that covers all of them.

**Applied:** R-API-055 (Who), [user-avatars.md](../security/user-avatars.md); `internal/api/v1/avatar_api.go` (`avatarOwner`; the scope check moved to the shared step by Q-API-214). Tests: `TestR_API_055_AvatarRefusals`.

### Q-API-214 · The operations on the caller's own account declare that a token must inherit its owner's rights

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: Q-API-213 closed the gap for the avatar in the handler. The routes of the UI preferences (`updatePreferences`), the own sessions (`endOwnSession`, `endOwnSessions`, `listOwnSessions`) and `revokeOwnTokens` declare `authenticated: true` and check at most the kind of the principal, so a token narrowed by R-AUTH-024 to one repository or one capability could change its owner's preferences, end the owner's sessions (including the browser session) and revoke all the owner's tokens. A scope is a ceiling that holds only where a handler remembers to apply it, and a new `users/me` write could forget it again.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A helper per handler | `avatarOwner`'s check becomes `requireOwnerRights(r)`, called by each handler | No change to the document or the shared step | The class stays open: a handler that does not call it is open, and nothing finds it |
| (b) A route attribute `x-trove-owner-rights: required`, read at load and enforced by the shared step, plus a test that classifies every unsafe `authenticated` operation (chosen) | `Operation.OwnerRights`; `authorize` refuses a token whose `Credential.Scope` is set and not `Inherit` with `403 forbidden` after the permission decision, like `RecentAuth`; any value but `required`, the attribute on a declaration other than `authenticated: true`, and the attribute on an operation of `/files/` or of the content routes (decided by the files handler, which the shared step never wraps) stops start-up | The document is what runs (as for Q-API-40 and the CI gate); the handlers lose their copies; the classification test makes a new `authenticated` write a deliberate decision | One more extension; a new operation needs a line in the test or in the document |
| (c) The refusal as the default for every unsafe `authenticated` operation, with an `admitted` opt-out in the document | As the CI gate (Q-CI-18) | Closed by construction | About a dozen operations that decide through the decision point or the token rules (package owners, mirror run, job cancel, token creation, rotation, `authz/check`) would each need a declaration that says nothing; the runtime step cannot tell them from an own-account write |
| (d) Sessions only | Tokens refused on the own-account operations | The strictest | A script with a full personal token loses what Q-API-213 kept for the avatar; the API would have browser-only writes |

**Choice:** (b). The attribute is on `setAvatar`, `removeAvatar`, `updatePreferences`, `listOwnSessions`, `endOwnSession`, `endOwnSessions` and `revokeOwnTokens`. `TestR_API_021_EveryAuthenticatedWriteDeclaresItsTokenRule` walks the document: every operation with an unsafe method and `authenticated: true` either declares `x-trove-owner-rights` or is in `ownerRightsExempt` with the reason (it decides through the decision point, which applies the scope; or its own rule applies: derivation R-AUTH-027, the line of revocation and rotation R-AUTH-029 and R-AUTH-030 (Q-AUTH-199), the presenting token itself, the scope's `manage` for an owner change (Q-AUTHZ-240), a session or an inheriting token for the starter of a job (Q-API-215)), and the set that declares it is compared with the list above. Reads of the own profile (`getCurrentUser`, `getPreferences`, `getWhoami`, `getAuthzMe`) stay open to every token: they return what the credential may know about itself and the UI needs them. The session list is in the set because it shows the addresses and user agents of the owner's other logins, which no scope names. The reads are classified the same way: `TestR_API_021_EveryAuthenticatedReadIsClassified` walks every authenticated `GET`, which either declares the attribute or is in `ownerRightsReads` with the reason it may answer a narrowed token (the credential's own data, a filter with the token's scope, or nothing of the account). The one read that shows the owner's activity beyond the credential, the job list and a job, stays open by Q-API-215 so a pipeline polls the run it started. A token with `admin: true` and `inherit: false` is a narrowed token here: the flag is about the owner's personal rights, not about administration. The attribute takes away no capability the scope names: an administrator's token with `admin: true`, or a scope naming `identities:read`, `identities:write` or `tokens:revoke` with an owner whose roles grant it, still lists and ends the owner's sessions, removes the owner's avatar and revokes the owner's tokens through `/api/v1/users/{username}/…` with the owner's own name, as it does for every user; that is the capability, not an escalation past the rule.

**Rationale:** the avatar decision (Q-API-213) chose "inherit or session" and the same reasoning holds for every operation on the owner's own account, so the mechanism, not the list, is the decision. The attribute follows the shape of `x-trove-recent-auth` (Q-API-40), which solved the same problem of a rule the document states but a handler may forget. The development agent would revisit (c) if the exempt list grows beyond what a reviewer can hold. Three more operations admitted a narrowed token by its owner's identity, and their rules need the record of the target, so they cannot be a route attribute; each is decided on the page of its rule and named in the exempt list: the token operations (`listTokens`, `getToken`, `revokeToken`, `rotateToken`) reach only the token's line, itself and the tokens derived from it ([Q-AUTH-199](identity-and-authentication.md#q-auth-199--a-token-whose-scope-does-not-inherit-sees-revokes-and-rotates-only-itself-and-the-tokens-derived-from-it)); an owner of a package name changes its owners through such a token only where the scope lists `manage` on the name ([Q-AUTHZ-240](authorization.md#q-authz-240--an-owner-changes-the-owners-of-a-name-through-a-narrowed-token-only-where-its-scope-lists-manage-on-the-name)); the one who started a job cancels it through such a token only with `settings:write` (Q-API-215).

**Applied:** R-API-002 (table of declarations), R-API-021, R-API-055; R-AUTH-024 and R-AUTH-010 in [identity-and-authentication.md](identity-and-authentication.md); `api/openapi.yaml` (the attribute on seven operations), `internal/api/v1/document.go` (`Operation.OwnerRights`, `parseOwnerRights`), `internal/api/v1/authorize.go` (`ownerRightsGate`), `internal/api/v1/avatar_api.go` (the handler's own check removed). Tests: `TestR_API_021_DocumentDeclaresOwnerRights`, `TestR_API_021_EveryAuthenticatedWriteDeclaresItsTokenRule`, `TestR_API_021_EveryAuthenticatedReadIsClassified`, `TestR_API_021_TheAttributeIsRefusedOnTheOperationsOfTheFilesHandler`, `TestR_API_021_ANarrowedTokenIsRefusedOnTheOperationsOfTheOwnAccount`, `TestR_API_021_TheRegisteredRoutesCarryTheGate`, `TestR_API_021_TheReadsOfTheOwnProfileAdmitANarrowedToken` (unit), `TestR_API_021_ANarrowedTokenDoesNotChangeItsOwnersAccount` (integration), `TestR_API_055_AvatarRefusals`.

### Q-API-215 · The one who started a job cancels it through a session or a token that inherits its rights

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: `POST /api/v1/system/jobs/{id}/cancel` admits a holder of `settings:write` and the caller who started the job
(R-API-015). The second way in compares the principal ID with `job.created_by`, so a token whose scope does not inherit its
owner's rights cancelled every job its owner started through a session or another token: a mirror run, a vulnerability
rescan, a task the owner ran as an administrator. It is the class of Q-API-214 on a rule of this page. The job row records
the principal, not the token (`created_by`, no token column), so the line of Q-AUTH-199 cannot be applied as it is.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The starter's way in admits a session and an inheriting token; a narrowed token cancels only through `settings:write` (chosen) | One condition in `mayCancel`; reading the job stays open | No schema change; the same "inherit or session" rule as the own-account operations; `settings:write` named by the scope still works | A pipeline whose narrowed token started a mirror run cannot cancel it; it waits for the run to end, or the owner cancels it |
| (b) Record the starting token on the job and let a token cancel the jobs its line started | A column `created_by_token` and the lineage read of Q-AUTH-199 | A narrowed token cancels what it started | A column and a migration for a convenience; every job-starting path has to pass the token; the jobs of a session would need a marker of their own |
| (c) Refuse the starter's way to every token | Sessions only | The strictest | A script with a full token loses the cancel it has today |
| (d) Leave it | The principal decides | No change | A leaked narrowed token stops its owner's long-running work |

**Choice:** (a). A token is narrowed when its scope does not inherit the owner's rights (`inherit: false`, also with
`admin: true`). The refusal is 403 with a detail that names the rule; a job the caller may not see at all stays 404
(Q-API-23). Reading the job and the job list keep the starter's way for every credential: a token that started a job polls
it through the `Location` of its 202, and the read changes nothing.

**Rationale:** the scope is a promise that a token does only what it was made for; stopping the owner's other work is not
that, and recording the token on every job would cost a schema change for the narrow case of a narrowed token cancelling
its own run. The development agent would revisit (b) if pipelines need to cancel the runs their tokens start.

**Applied:** R-API-015 (rule, acceptance); `internal/api/v1/jobs_api.go` (`mayCancel`), `api/openapi.yaml` (`cancelJob`),
[tokens-and-credentials.md](../security/tokens-and-credentials.md). Tests: `TestR_API_015_TheStarterCancelsThroughASessionOrAnInheritingToken`
(unit), `TestR_API_015_ANarrowedTokenCancelsItsOwnersJobsOnlyWithSettingsWrite` (integration).

### Q-UI-172 · The jobs table shows a job's error code, its detail and the attempt it failed in, in the result cell

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the result cell showed only `error.code` of a failed job, so the owner's jobs screen said `job_failed` for 58 runs whose
cause was in the job's `detail` the API returned ([vulnerability-scanning.md](vulnerability-scanning.md) Q-VULN-121). The detail is
at most 2,000 bytes; a failed sync's is a sentence or two. The table serves the jobs screen and the recent jobs of the status
screen. The owner's direction is to copy GitLab and add no unasked styling; GitLab's job list names a failure reason in a tooltip
and its job page shows the log.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The code only, as built | — | Compact rows | The screen does not name the cause |
| (b) The code, the detail and "Attempt *n* of *m*" in the result cell, the detail wrapping at any character (chosen) | Every row with an error shows it | Visible without a click, readable by a screen reader in reading order, no state; a long entry name cannot widen the table | A row with a long detail is tall |
| (c) The code and a disclosure "Show the error" that opens the detail | Rows stay short | Compact | One click per failure for the one thing the owner looked for; a disclosure per row is state the refresh every 5 s must keep |
| (d) A tooltip with the detail, as GitLab's list | Hover | Compact | Not reachable by keyboard and touch without extra work, and not read in order; 2,000 bytes do not fit a tooltip |
| (e) A page per job | A route `/admin/system/jobs/{id}` | Room for the result too | A new screen for two lines of text |

**Choice:** (b). *n* is the error's `attempt`, the attempt the detail belongs to (a job queued or running again carries the error
of the attempt before), else the job's `attempt`; *m* is `maxAttempts`. The code and the detail are not translated (`translate="no"`);
the attempt line is.
**Rationale:** the cause of a failure is what an operator opens the jobs screen for, and failures are the exception in the list, so
the room they take is room where it is needed. The development agent would revisit this if lists with many long details become hard
to scan, with a clamp to a few lines and a control to expand.
**Applied:** R-UI-038 (the Jobs bullet); [operations-and-observability.md](operations-and-observability.md) Q-OPS-186 types the
members. Code: `web/src/app/features/system/job-table.ts`; the manual page [operations.md](../manual/admin/operations.md#jobs).

### Q-UI-173 · The slowest accepted avatar is measured against the decode deadline and pinned in the performance run

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: finding F-81. The area limit accepts 2048 x 2048 pixels (4,194,304) and a decode is cut off after 5 s (`avatar.DecodeTimeout`), but the only test of the largest accepted area raised the deadline to one minute, because Test and Release run 42409044656 measured 9.7 s for a 2048 x 2048 PNG under the race detector on a throttled runner. Nothing showed that an image the checks accept decodes inside 5 s without the race detector in a CPU-limited pod. The chart gives the pods that serve `/api/v1/` (the `api` and `all` roles) a CPU request of 500m and no CPU limit (`deploy/helm/trove/values.yaml`, `api.resources`); an operator may set one, and a replica decodes two images at a time (`MaxConcurrent`), so under load each decode gets half of what the pod gets.

What decides the slowest accepted image depends on the format. For a PNG, a baseline JPEG and a WebP the 1 MiB upload cap does: a 2048 x 2048 PNG of 16 bits per channel is 32 MiB of filtered rows, so it is accepted only when it deflates at least 32 to 1, and noise that does not compress is refused by size before any decoder runs. The slowest are the images with the most work per byte: Paeth on every row, Adam7 interlacing, 16 bits, sparse noise that keeps the deflate stream literal-heavy. For a progressive JPEG the cap does not decide: the cost is the area times the scans times the work of a scan, and a scan can be a few bytes. The first version of this decision assumed the cap decided for every format and missed that (found in review, with a deadline that did not fire for such a file); [Q-UI-174](api-and-ui.md#q-ui-174--the-scans-of-a-jpeg-are-bounded-by-block-visits-and-the-decoders-input-is-read-in-short-pieces) bounds it.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Build the slowest accepted inputs in code, measure them without the race detector in a CPU-limited cgroup, and pin the property in the performance run (chosen) | `internal/avatar/worstcase_test.go`; `make test-performance` | Shows the claim of the security page with numbers and found the unbounded JPEG case; costs the user nothing | The numbers are one machine's; a different CPU needs a new reading |
| (b) Lower `MaxPixels` (1024 x 1024) | Four times fewer pixels | Four times less CPU for the worst case | Refuses ordinary 1,500 px photos for a 256 px result; the measurement shows no need |
| (c) Raise `DecodeTimeout` (10 s or more) | A starved pod finishes more decodes | Fewer `too_complex` for legitimate images on a starved pod | Holds a decoding slot and a CPU for twice as long per hostile upload: the deadline is the bound of what an upload costs (H-560), so a larger one is a weaker defence for a case the measurement does not show |
| (d) Decode at reduced resolution (a DCT-scaled JPEG decode, a subsampled PNG) | Less work per image | Lower worst case | The standard library has no scaled decode; PNG has none at all; a second decoder is more attack surface than the problem |
| (e) Measure the deadline in CPU time, not wall time | A starved pod is not penalised | Independent of the host's load | Go has no per-goroutine CPU clock; the process's CPU time includes the other request on the replica |

**Choice:** (a). Measured on 2026-11-08 in `golang:1.27.3` (linux/arm64, a 20-CPU Docker VM), without `-race`, `docker run --cpus=1` (Go then runs two threads), `BenchmarkProcessWorstCase` (decode, centre-square scale and PNG encode of the whole `Process`), 8 samples of each, at a host load average of 14 to 23 on 20 cores (the host is shared; the readings of the same inputs in the hours before, at 33 to 128, were more than 25 times slower in the worst sample, which is why the floor, not a median, is the image's cost). The 3-component JPEGs are at 1,576 x 1,576, the 4-component at the largest side the memory estimate admits (1,392 x 1,392); the "visit limit" inputs spend `MaxBlockVisits` exactly (Q-UI-174).

| Slowest accepted input (bytes of 1,048,576) | Floor, CPU | Median, wall | Maximum, wall |
|---|---|---|---|
| PNG 16-bit RGBA, Adam7, Paeth, noise (978,235) | 292 ms | 296 ms | 301 ms |
| PNG 16-bit RGBA, Paeth, noise (973,794) | 272 ms | 276 ms | 301 ms |
| PNG 8-bit RGBA, Adam7, Paeth, noise (1,005,666) | 171 ms | 173 ms | 193 ms |
| WebP lossless, one bit of noise a pixel, no transform (524,322) | 244 ms | 246 ms | 268 ms |
| JPEG baseline, noise, highest quality that fits (1,047,075) | 144 ms | 148 ms | 157 ms |
| JPEG progressive, gray, 10 scans, dense (1,027,877) | 149 ms | 150 ms | 158 ms |
| JPEG progressive, gray, 48 scans, dense, at the visit limit (671,682) | 436 ms | 438 ms | 442 ms |
| JPEG progressive, 3 components, 10 scans, dense (866,014) | 201 ms | 204 ms | 211 ms |
| JPEG progressive, 3 components, 64 scans, dense (691,995) | 441 ms | 447 ms | 466 ms |
| JPEG progressive, gray, 1 DC and 23 AC refinement scans of end-of-band runs, at the limit (8,760) | 310 ms | 314 ms | 317 ms |
| JPEG progressive, gray, 48 DC scans, at the limit (393,840) | 417 ms | 422 ms | 432 ms |
| JPEG progressive, 3 components, 27 interleaved DC scans, at the limit (393,486) | 440 ms | 454 ms | 500 ms |
| JPEG progressive, 3 components, 1 DC and 39 AC refinement scans, at the limit (15,342) | 338 ms | 342 ms | 356 ms |
| JPEG progressive, 4 components, 25 interleaved DC scans, at the limit (379,019) | 457 ms | 467 ms | 475 ms |

The slowest accepted image costs about 0.47 s of CPU. One decode therefore needs 0.094 CPU on average to finish inside 5 s, and a pod that runs two such decodes at once (an attacker fills both slots) needs 0.19 CPU. As a limit of 500m (the chart's request, which is not a limit) that is 0.25 CPU per decode and a predicted 1.9 s for the slowest, a margin of 2.6; that figure is the CPU time divided by the share, not a reading: the runs with `--cpus=0.5` fell in the loaded hours and are not reported. The scale and the encode are part of every figure; the lossy WebP is not measured (the repository has no encoder to build one) and a lossless WebP with transforms (predictor, cross-colour, subtract-green), which adds work per pixel for almost no bytes, was not built, so the WebP row is the stream without them, not the slowest. Only linux/arm64 and the development machine's CPU were measured.

The race detector took 9.7 s for a 2048 x 2048 PNG on a throttled runner (Test and Release run 42409044656) that takes about 0.3 s without it, which is why the per-change tier, which runs with it, judges none of this: both tests skip under `-race` (building the inputs alone takes minutes there). They are not part of the plain run of `make test` either, because the inputs take 14 s to build, and that is paid on every change for a property that moves only when the decoders or the bounds do; `make test-performance`, the nightly run, runs them without `-race`. `TestR_API_055_TheWorstCaseInputsAreAccepted` checks that each input fits the cap, passes every check and decodes. `TestR_API_055_TheSlowestAcceptedImagesDecodeInsideTheDeadline` decodes each input with a deadline of a minute (a slow decode on a busy host is a reading, not a refusal) and logs wall and CPU time; with `TROVE_PERF_GATE=1` it decodes each input seven times (the inputs are built once) and requires the least CPU time inside one second, the threshold of the revisit condition below. The wall time is logged and not judged: on a shared runner it is the runner's load (under a load of 36 to 77 on 20 cores at `--cpus=1` the median wall time of three fresh decodes was 3.3 to 5.0 s while the benchmark floor was 0.58 to 0.9 s, each fresh decode also paying a collection of the 40 MB it allocates), which is the lesson of Q-ARCH-220; the least of several CPU readings is the image's cost, and H-641 turns that into the CPU a pod needs. The inputs are deterministic and fit the cap by construction.

**Rationale:** for a PNG, a baseline JPEG and a WebP the numbers show a margin of 15 or more on an unlimited pod, and no bound has to move; for a progressive JPEG the number of scans was not a bound, which Q-UI-174 corrects. Lowering the area or raising the deadline would change what users and attackers get for a risk the measurement does not show. The development agent revisits the numbers when the floor of any row above exceeds 1 s on the platform's reference hardware (then the area, `MaxBlockVisits` or `MaxScans` falls, not the deadline), when an operator reports `too_complex` for ordinary images (then the CPU limit of the pod is the cause: H-641), when a decoder is replaced, or when a lossless WebP with transforms is built and costs more than a row above.
**Applied:** R-API-055 (Bounded cost); [user-avatars.md](../security/user-avatars.md) (the cost section, H-640, H-641); `internal/avatar/worstcase_test.go`, `worstcase_bench_unix_test.go`, `cpu_unix_test.go`, `cpu_other_test.go`, `race_on_test.go`, `race_off_test.go`; `Makefile` (`test-performance`); [build-and-test.md](../developer/build-and-test.md), [identity.md](../developer/identity.md).

### Q-UI-174 · The scans of a JPEG are bounded by block visits, and the decoder's input is read in short pieces

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the review of Q-UI-173 found two things that the number of scans (`MaxScans`, 64, Q-API-211) does not bound. (1) The standard decoder walks every block of every component of a scan, for each scan, and checks only that a refinement scan follows one with one bit less, so a scan can repeat. A progressive JPEG whose scans are interleaved DC scans over three or four components, or AC refinement scans of one band in end-of-band runs, costs the same per scan whether the scan is a megabyte or seven bytes. Measured by the reviewer in `golang:1.27.3` at `--cpus=1`: four components at 1,392 x 1,392 with 64 interleaved DC scans (970,025 bytes) 1,011 ms of CPU, three components at 1,576 x 1,576 with 64 DC scans 958 to 990 ms, gray 2048 x 2048 with one DC and 63 AC refinement scans (9,480 bytes) 745 ms, against 550 ms for the densest 64-scan file of the first version. (2) The deadline is looked at only when the decoder reads: the decoders fill a buffer of 4 KiB, so the 9,480-byte file is read in about three reads, all its scans run after the last one, and a deadline of 50 ms ended with the image decoded in 878 ms and no error (reproduced here: 5 ms, 159 ms, no error). The first finding breaks the premise of Q-UI-173 for JPEG, and the second makes the deadline no bound for that class.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A budget of block visits summed over the scans in `walkJPEG`, AC refinement counted twice, refused before a slot is taken, and reads of the decoder's input cut to 16 bytes (chosen) | `MaxBlockVisits` = 3,145,728 = 48 scans of the 65,536 blocks of a 2048 x 2048 component; `readChunk` = 16 | Bounds the work from the header, so a hostile file never holds a slot or a CPU; scales with the components and the area as the cost does; the short reads make the deadline fire inside the scans | A constant calibrated by measurement; the factor two for refinement is flat, not by band width |
| (b) Lower `MaxScans` (to 24) | One number | Simple | Counts a scan of a gray image as much as one of a four-component image, which cost four times as much; refuses a gray file of 30 scans that costs a third of the allowance |
| (c) Only the short reads | The deadline is looked at inside the scans | Smallest change | A hostile upload then costs the full deadline of CPU on a slot, 5 s, before it is refused; the work is not bounded from the header |
| (d) A visit budget weighted by the band width of a refinement scan | Closer to the cost | More exact | A header field more to parse and calibrate for a difference of less than two |
| (e) Leave it | — | — | The deadline and the scan count are not the bounds the security page claims |

**Choice:** (a). A scan visits every block of every component it carries, taken at the full resolution of the frame (an upper bound for a subsampled one); an AC refinement scan counts twice; more than 3,145,728 visits in all is `422` `too_complex`, like more than 64 scans. The reads of the decoder's input return at most 16 bytes: about 65,000 reads for a 1 MiB upload, each a context check. Measured at the limit (table in Q-UI-173) the costliest file is 0.47 s of CPU; a typical progressive photo of ten scans visits about a fifth of the allowance (655,360 for a 2048 x 2048 gray one). `TestR_API_055_RefusesAJPEGWhoseScansAddUpToTooMuchWork` refuses the inputs above (and the plans that spend the allowance exactly are accepted, one scan more is not) before a slot is taken; `TestR_API_055_StopsAScanHeavyDecodeAtItsDeadline` decodes the 8,760-byte refinement file at the limit with a deadline of 5 ms and 20 ms and requires `too_complex`, and fails with reads of a megabyte.

**Rationale:** the cost of a progressive JPEG is the area times the scans times the work of a scan, and only the header says the first two, so the budget is what the header can prove; the deadline stays as the bound for what the header cannot (H-640). The development agent revisits the constant when ordinary progressive photos are refused (the allowance is five times a typical photo's), when the floor of the file that spends it exceeds 1 s, or when the standard decoder gets a cheaper scan.
**Applied:** R-API-055 (the size and cost bullet, Bounded cost); [user-avatars.md](../security/user-avatars.md) (steps 6 and 8, the cost section, H-640); `internal/avatar/process.go` (`MaxBlockVisits`, `walkJPEG`, `scanVisits`, `readChunk`, `ctxReader`); `internal/avatar/budget_test.go`, `bounds_test.go`.


### Q-UI-177 · The facts of an OCI tag and the platforms of an index sit in the Metadata tab of the package page

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: R-OCI-031 gives an image name as a package and its tags as versions; the version `metadata` holds `digest`, `mediaType`, `size`, `artifactType` and, for an index, `platforms` (one object per child with `platform`, `digest`, `mediaType` and `size`). R-UI-007 names the tabs and says the Metadata tab is format-specific. An OCI tag has no README and no license, and the page's files tab lists the manifest the tag points at.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) An "Image" block and a "Platforms" table in the Metadata tab (chosen) | `dl` with digest (copy button), media type, artifact type, size; below it a table of the platforms | No new tab or route; the tab already is "the format's facts"; the same tab ids and `?tab=metadata` link for every format | The facts are not visible in the header: an image has no README, so the Metadata tab is its first tab and one click opens them |
| (b) A separate "Platforms" tab for indexes | One more tab id, shown only for an index | The table is one click from the header | A tab that exists for one format and for some versions; the tab list of R-UI-007 and its link vocabulary grow for it |
| (c) Put the digest and size in the header facts | The header shows them for every format | Visible at once | The header is the same for all formats and has no place for a column of 64-character digests |

**Choice:** (a). The block is read from the metadata members the view API sends and shows what is present: an absent artifact type or size shows no row, a tag whose metadata has no digest shows the empty-state sentence, a child without a string digest is not listed, and a child's size that is no number reads "–". The platform is shown as the server sends it, `unknown/unknown` for an attestation included, because the page must not interpret what the server has not marked; a child the index names without a platform (an empty string, the rows' COALESCE) reads "No platform". A provenance attestation exists once per platform and all are `unknown/unknown`, so a row whose platform is empty or repeated gets the first twelve hex digits of its digest after the platform, read by assistive technology only, and the same in the name of its copy button; every row header and every button name on the page is unique. Sizes use the binary units of the rest of the page; the copy buttons are named "Copy digest" for the tag and "Copy digest of <platform>" for a child.
**Rationale:** the Metadata tab is where the other formats show their format-specific facts, so a reader finds an image's facts where they find a package's dependencies. The development agent revisits this when the layer history or the labels are shown (Deferred in R-OCI-031): that content is large enough to deserve a tab of its own.
**Applied:** R-UI-007 (the Metadata bullet); `web/src/app/features/packages/package-detail.{ts,html}`, `package-detail.spec.ts`, `fakes-packages.ts` (`ociFixture`); [web-ui.md](../developer/web-ui.md).

### Q-UI-200 · An array of strings in a settings schema is a list control, a long string an area

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: the settings form (Q-UI-78) rendered an array as "This setting cannot be changed here. Set it through the API". Every list of the Debian settings (`architectures`, `compression`, `suites`, `components`, the five members of `mirror`) is an array of strings, and `upstreamKeys` is a block of up to 256 KiB.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A `list` control for an array of strings: a textarea with one entry per line, or a checkbox per option when the items are an enum; an empty list leaves the default; a string with `maxLength` above 1 KiB gets a textarea (chosen) | The schema alone decides; no format code in the form | Every format with such a list is editable at once (FMT-001); the same pruning against the default as for text (Q-UI-80) | Items are plain strings: a pattern of the schema is checked by the server, the form does not repeat it |
| (b) A chip input | One entry per chip | Familiar | A new control, keyboard handling and a test surface for what a textarea does |
| (c) A panel per format | Debian-specific form | Tailored | The UI would know a format (FMT-001) |

**Choice:** (a). A typed list keeps the text the user typed while it parses to the stored array, so a blank line being typed is not rewritten under the cursor. An array of anything but strings stays "other": shown, not edited. The fixture of the "other" case in the specs is now an array of objects, which is what that case always meant.
**Rationale:** the schema already says what the control is; a list is the commonest setting after text and a boolean. The development agent revisits this when a schema needs ordered entries with structure.
**Applied:** R-UI-021 (the list bullet); `web/src/app/features/repositories/settings-schema.ts`, `format-settings.ts` and their specs; `fakes-catalog.ts` (`DEB_SETTINGS_SCHEMA`).

### Q-UI-202 · The Debian key panel never keeps a secret it was given, and asks before it erases

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |

| (a) The import form holds the armored key and the passphrase in two fields (the passphrase is `type="password"`), sends them once and clears both after the answer, also a refusal; promote, remove and confirm-retirement ask first and say what they erase (chosen) | No secret is kept in a signal after the call, in storage, in the URL or in a draft | The smallest time a secret lives in the page; a refused key is pasted again, which is rare | Someone who mistypes a passphrase pastes the key again |
| (b) Keep the key in the form after a refusal | Retry without pasting | Convenient | The secret stays in the page as long as the form is open |
| (c) No confirmation | Fewer clicks | Faster | A promotion erases a private key and breaks every client that never replaced its key file |

### Q-API-235 · A scope is rendered and accepted only where the client has a scoped variant

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: `scope` of the client-setup operation was accepted for every format and `renderSnippets` added a `-scoped` copy of every
configure template, whatever the format. An OCI repository asked for a scope answered `docker.configure.shell-scoped` and
`docker.configure.kubernetes-scoped`, byte-identical copies of the unscoped snippets under an id that promises something the snippet
does not do. Only the npm templates read the variant (`SetupData.Variant`). The UI never sends `scope`, so the defect was dormant.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Copy only templates that read the variant | The renderer detects `.Variant` in the parse tree of a configure template; others render once | The ids are true | A request for a scope on OCI still answers 200 and silently ignores it |
| (b) Refuse `scope` with 400 for a client without a scoped variant | Same detection, used as a check | The caller learns that there is no such variant | Alone, it leaves a client with some templates that read the variant and some that do not rendering copies of the latter |
| (c) Both (chosen) | The check in the handler, the detection in the renderer | A scoped id always means a different snippet; a scope that cannot be honoured is an error, not a no-op | One walk of the parse tree per template and request |
| (d) A flag on `SetupTemplate` | The format declares the variant | Explicit | A second declaration that can disagree with the text; a change of the format contract (R-ARCH-025) |

**Choice:** (c), with the detection of (a)/(b) over the parse tree, not a flag (d). A configure template has a scoped variant when it
references `.Variant` or `$.Variant`; an install or publish template never has one. The handler answers `400 malformed_request` whose detail names `scope`
when no configure template of the requested client has a scoped variant. Today that is `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn` and `yarn-classic`.

**Rationale:** an API that answers 200 with the unscoped snippet to a scoped request lets a script believe it configured one scope
while it bound the whole client. Using the template itself as the declaration cannot disagree with the template. The development
agent revisits this when a format wants a scoped variant of a template that does not read `.Variant` (none is conceivable: the
variant is its content), or when the UI offers a scope input and needs to know in advance which clients take one (then the setup answer
would list them).

**Applied:** `hasScopedVariant`, `clientHasScopedVariant` and the check in `clientSetup` ([setup_snippets.go](../../internal/api/v1/setup_snippets.go), [packages_api.go](../../internal/api/v1/packages_api.go)); the description of `scope` in [openapi.yaml](../../api/openapi.yaml); R-API-030 above;
[packages.md](../developer/packages.md); `TestR_API_030_OnlyAConfigureTemplateThatReadsTheVariantComesTwice`, `TestR_API_030_TheScopedVariantIsDetectedInEveryTemplateConstruct`, `TestR_API_030_ClientSetupRefusesWhatItCannotAnswer`, and the fixture test `TestR_API_030_RenderedSnippetIdsMatchTheUIFixture`, which renders every format with a scope.

### Q-API-238 · The read after a create honours Retry-After of an unconfirmed authorization state

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: finding F-90. `TestRepositoryResourceContract` (two replicas, every request sent to the other replica than the one before) failed once on a host with a load of 50 to 70 on 20 cores: the `GET` on the `Location` of a create answered not 200. Reproduced on the base commit with `-count=60` and 16 to 24 busy processes added (one failure in 54 runs, the first create of a fresh pair of replicas): the answer was `503 authz_stale`, "The authorization state of this replica could not be confirmed; retry", from the replica that had not created the repository, while its readiness checks for the database and the object store were timing out. It was not a `404` and not a stale body, so the repository itself was visible: R-API-052's rule that a management read comes from PostgreSQL held, and the catch-up of the grant index (R-ARCH-011 step 2, `Engine.CatchUp`) did what it is specified to do when it cannot finish in its budget, which the integration stack sets to `database.retry.max_elapsed` = 2 s (`test/integration/testenv/stack.go`; 30 s by default). Not measured: how long the index build took on that run.

On this sequence two bounded answers exist. `503 authz_stale` with `Retry-After` comes from the catch-up of the grant index when its budget ends. `503 unavailable` with `Retry-After: 1` comes from the repository reader (`SnapshotReader.lookup`) when `repositories.lookup_wait` (5 s) ends before the change-log poll answered. Outside this sequence `authz_stale` means something else: the replica's change-log poll has stalled for longer than the staleness bound of R-AUTHZ-028 and the index cannot be confirmed.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The read-back after a create repeats a `503 authz_stale` with `Retry-After`, for at most 30 s (chosen) | Only the `GET` that `create()` and the Location check send right after a create; only that code with a `Retry-After`; every other call of the contract answers at once | States the promise as the spec makes it, where the spec makes it (a repository the replica has just learned of); a stalled replica anywhere else in the suite still fails at its first `503`; each repeat is logged, so a suite that needs one for every create shows it; no timing bound of the product moves | The read-back waits where it used to fail, so a host slower than the budget shows as a log line and a long test, not a red one |
| (a2) The same repeat for every `GET` of `RunContract` | Five callers (api, authz, endpoints, identity, transfer) | One place | Outside the catch-up, `authz_stale` is a stalled poll, a real fault that the repeat would absorb in the traversal, ETag and patch tests |
| (a3) Also repeat `503 unavailable` | Covers the reader's lookup wait | The other form of F-90 would be absorbed too | `unavailable` is the generic code of every outage (database, object store, Valkey); repeating it would hide real ones. It is not repeated, so F-90 can recur in this form: a read-back that finds the reader's 5 s wait spent fails with that `503` |
| (b) Raise `database.retry.max_elapsed` of the stack | The replica waits longer for the index | Smallest edit | Moves a bound to fit the host and hides the cause (a build that needs more than 2 s) behind a larger number; the 2 s is what makes the test see a slow build at all |
| (c) Make the create wait until every replica's grant index holds the repository | The `201` answers later | Removes the `503` for this sequence | The creating replica cannot know the other replicas; a poll of all of them is a coordination mechanism the spec does not have (R-ARCH-018 is pull-based), and it would still not cover a build that fails on the other replica |
| (d) Run the test again until it passes | — | None | Hides a real defect |

**Choice:** (a). `suite.readBack` in `internal/api/v1/apitest/contract.go` sends the read-back again after the `Retry-After` of a `503` with the problem code `authz_stale` (50 ms when it is 0), until 30 s have passed, and logs every repeat with the status, `X-Trove-Replica`, the attempt number and the time waited; the `503` is then the answer. The bound is a client's: a replica that has not confirmed its state within its own wait (30 s by default) is stalled, so a client that has waited as long again has seen the answer twice. `call` does not repeat anything. The failure message of the Location check carries the status, the replica and the body. `TestReadBackIsRepeatedAfterRetryAfterOfAnUnconfirmedState`, `TestReadBackRepeatsOnlyAStaleAnswerWithRetryAfter`, `TestReadBackEndsWithTheAnswerOfAReplicaThatNeverConfirms` and `TestOtherCallsOfTheContractAreNotRepeated` pin the helper. The promise that a fresh repository is usable on the other replica at once, with no repeat, stays pinned by `test/integration/transfer/repository_api_test.go`.

**Rationale:** the product already keeps its promise (no `404` for a new repository, a body read from PostgreSQL); what a loaded host changes is whether the grant index of the answering replica is confirmed within 2 s, and the specified answer to "not yet" is a retryable `503`. The repeat is limited to the one place where the spec says a replica may legitimately not be ready. F-90 can still recur as `503 unavailable` (option a3). The development agent revisits this when the replica's catch-up is found to need more than the stack's 2 s on an idle host (then the build, not the test, is the finding), when the repeat is logged for most creates of a run, or when a client of the product other than the contract helper meets the `503` on this sequence in practice.
**Applied:** R-API-004 (acceptance criterion); `internal/api/v1/apitest/contract.go` (`readBack`, `staleBudget`), `internal/api/v1/apitest/call_test.go`; [http-api.md](../developer/http-api.md) (the tests step of the extension checklist).

### Q-UI-210 · The member editor is a tab with its own save, offers what the API accepts, and explains the saved order

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: R-UI-022 asks for two listboxes, five buttons, an effective resolution order that flattens nested virtual repositories, a default deployment target, a live region and the member of a 422 marked. The repository screen saves one document with one button; nested virtual repositories (R-REPO-018) and an `effectiveMembers` member do not exist (a virtual member answers `invalid_member`).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The members join the form of the General tab | One dirty state, one Save | One button | A reorder would be mixed with the settings of the other tabs; the conflict dialog compares whole forms |
| (b) A tab "Members" with its own Save, patching `virtual.members` and `virtual.deployTarget` only (chosen) | The patch carries these two members with the loaded `ETag`; the form's other edits stay | The editor is one component with one purpose; the 412 and the 422 belong to it | Two save buttons on one screen |
| (c) A separate route | `/repositories/<key>/members` | Own address | The repository detail has the stored document, the `ETag` and the permission already |

**Choice:** (b). [virtual-members.ts](../../web/src/app/features/repositories/virtual-members.ts) offers the repositories of the same project and format that are local or remote, not the repository itself, not a member and not being deleted (a virtual repository never lists another project's repository, Q-REPO-212; a virtual member is refused by the API, so none is offered, which is also what excludes a cycle today). The buttons Add, Remove, Move up, Move down and Move to top work with the pointer and with Enter or Space on a focused button; Alt with the arrow up or down key and Alt with Home move the selected member inside the list; drag and drop is not built (it is optional in R-UI-022 and every drag has the buttons, WCAG 2.5.7). The live region says "npm-remote moved to position 2 of 3", "added at position", "removed". Removing the member that is the default deployment target clears the target and says so. A 422 whose pointer is `/virtual/members/<n>` is shown on that member with `aria-invalid`; any other refusal is the error notice; a 412 offers "Load the stored repository". The effective resolution order is the saved member list with the deployment target marked, because nothing is nested yet; the explanation of a path is `GET …/resolution?path=` shown as a table of members and decisions, in words for every decision the document lists.

**Rationale:** the editor cannot show a flattening the API cannot produce, and a tab with its own save keeps a reorder from being swallowed by an unrelated edit. The development agent would revisit the flattening when R-REPO-018 is built and the API returns `effectiveMembers`, and the drag option if the owner asks for it.

**Applied in the spec:** none (R-UI-022 is met within these bounds). Code: [virtual-members.ts](../../web/src/app/features/repositories/virtual-members.ts), [repository-detail.ts](../../web/src/app/features/repositories/repository-detail.ts) (`saveMembers`), [repositories-api.ts](../../web/src/app/api/repositories-api.ts) (`resolution`). Tests: [virtual-members.spec.ts](../../web/src/app/features/repositories/virtual-members.spec.ts), the journey [18-virtual-members.spec.ts](../../web/e2e/tests/18-virtual-members.spec.ts) (CI, kind).

### Q-UI-211 · General settings save the banner and the mode separately, ask before read-only, and the shell reads both every 30 seconds

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: R-UI-033 shows the base URL, the banner and the maintenance mode on `/admin/settings/general`, and asks that an enabled banner appears on every screen for every user within a minute after saving. R-OPS-025 asks that the sign-in page shows it. The banner store was a stub with no API behind it.

**Choice:** [general-settings.ts](../../web/src/app/features/settings/general-settings.ts) has one form and one Save for the banner (enabled, severity, optional title, message with a preview that shows only `https` links) and one for the mode (switch, message, cache-fill switch, retry hint), because they are two documents. Switching the mode on opens a confirmation that says every user's writes are refused; switching it off does not. A caller without `settings:write` sees the values in a disabled fieldset with the reason. [banner-store.ts](../../web/src/app/core/banner-store.ts) reads `GET /system/banner` for everyone and `GET /system/maintenance` for a signed-in caller when a screen with the banner starts watching and every 30 s ([BANNER_POLL_MS](../../web/src/app/core/banner-store.ts)); a save puts the answer into the store at once, so the writer sees it without waiting. [banner.ts](../../web/src/app/shared/banner.ts) is in the shell and on the sign-in page; severity is an icon and a word as well as the colours of the badge tokens, the maintenance notice comes first. The message is bound as text and as `href` of `https` links only; a link to anything else stays in the text as typed ([banner-text.ts](../../web/src/app/shared/banner-text.ts)). The sidebar gets the entry "General settings".

**Rationale:** one poll of 30 s meets the minute with room for a missed one and costs a request per signed-in tab per half minute, answered from PostgreSQL by a primary-key read of two rows. The development agent would revisit the poll if the load shows or if the system notification channel (a server-sent stream) is built.

**Applied in the spec:** none (R-UI-033, R-OPS-025). Code as linked. Tests: [general-settings.spec.ts](../../web/src/app/features/settings/general-settings.spec.ts), [banner-store.spec.ts](../../web/src/app/core/banner-store.spec.ts), [banner.spec.ts](../../web/src/app/shared/banner.spec.ts), the journey [19-general-settings.spec.ts](../../web/e2e/tests/19-general-settings.spec.ts) (CI, kind).

Context: the acceptance criterion of R-UI-047 asks that a deliberately broken snippet template fails the end-to-end client-setup test. The journey of Q-UI-82 compares the page with the snippets of the npm matrix written out in the journey, character for character. Nothing showed that a broken template makes that comparison fail, and a cluster run that rebuilds the image with a broken template for it is expensive and tests the comparison, not the template.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A kind run with a broken template | Build an image with a mutated template, run the journey, expect red | The literal criterion | An image build and a cluster run for a fact a string comparison decides; the run would need an inverted result in the report |
| (b) A test on the renderer with the journey's texts and mutated templates (chosen) | `renderSnippets` renders the real npm templates for the journey's data and equals the written-out texts; six mutations (a dropped registry line, a dropped credential line, a misspelled key, a lost newline, a lost always-auth switch, an unwritten URL) each differ | The proof runs on every pull request; the comparison is the journey's, so what fails here fails there | The texts are written down a third time |

**Choice:** (b). The journey stays as Q-UI-82 decided; the Go test carries the same four texts.

### Q-UI-213 · The token form names what a token can be in three choices, and only an administrator is offered the first

Status: **Decided by the owner** (2026-11-10), on a proposal of the development agent.

Context: the owner created a personal token with **All permissions of the owner** and `docker push` answered `denied`. The form sent `{"inherit": true}`, which R-AUTH-024 defines as the owner's repository permissions without administration, and the owner holds no repository permission other than through the administrator role, so the registry token carried no `push`. The label promised more than the token held, and the form had no way to set `admin: true`.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Three radio buttons (chosen) | **Administrator: everything on this installation**, only for a caller with the role; **All repository permissions of the owner, without administration**, preselected; **Only the repositories and actions below** | Only valid states; the list uses the same words | One more line in the form |
| (b) The radio buttons plus an administrator checkbox | A switch beside the scope | Closest to the two API fields | Administrator rights next to a repository list reads as a limit, while `content:bypass` passes every repository check |
| (c) A token of an administrator is one by default | `{"inherit": true, "admin": true}` when no scope is given | Nothing to choose | Every token an administrator makes without thinking administers the installation, also one in a CI secret |

**Choice:** (a). The first choice sends `{"inherit": true, "admin": true}`, so that the token also acts on the owner's own account (R-AUTH-024). **Rationale:** a token is one of three things, and a control that can only be in those three states cannot promise what the token does not hold. The default of R-AUTH-024 stands: administrator power is an explicit choice.

**A token is not revoked when its owner loses the role** (recommended by the development agent; the owner did not object). The role is checked at every use (R-AUTHZ-010), so the power ends with the role. A revocation would add nothing to that and would end every such token for good if one login through the identity provider carried no group claim (R-AUTH-008). What remains is that the token holds the power again if the owner regains the role; its lifetime bounds that, and the list of the owner's tokens says that the rights are inactive.

Not covered at the time: the form of a service-account token offered no administrator rights (the account's role was not known to the form), and the token administration (R-UI-030) did not know the role of each owner, so it showed no such notice. Both are built since ([Q-UI-220](#q-ui-220--the-form-of-a-service-account-token-offers-the-administrator-choice-for-an-account-that-holds-the-role), [Q-UI-221](#q-ui-221--the-token-administration-marks-administrator-tokens-whose-owner-no-longer-holds-the-role), on the fields of [Q-AUTH-209](identity-and-authentication.md#q-auth-209--a-token-and-a-service-account-state-whether-the-owner-holds-the-administrator-role)).

**Applied in the spec:** R-UI-029. Code: `TokenForm` and `scopeSummary` in `web/src/app/shared/access/`.

Context: the screen showed `user:name` in a plain table with a labelled select per row and a form below the list. The reference shows an account with avatar, name and user name, its source, its role and a row menu, under a tab with the count and a filter bar; adding is a dialog behind a button at the top right.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |

| (a) The reference's layout with what trove knows (chosen) | Header with **Add member**, tab with the count, filter and sort, columns Account, Source and Role, a row menu, the add form in a dialog; `GET /api/v1/projects/{key}/members` carries `id`, `displayName` and `avatarUrl` | The reference's reading order, with real people instead of references | The list answer grows by three members |

Every project reader sees the display name and the avatar of the project's members: the avatar image is available to every authenticated caller by its digest (R-API-055), and the display name comes from the identity provider and is shown to the same readers next to the user name they already see. **Rationale:** the reference's list is about people, and a list of references is not. The source is always **Direct member**, because a project has no other kind of membership. The badge **It's you** is blue, not the reference's green, because green is a positive status alone (Q-UI-96). The development agent would add Expiration or Activity with a feature that stores them.

### Q-UI-215 · Settings are fields in one column, and everything that folds is animated

Status: **Decided by the owner** (2026-11-10): the screenshot of the reference's general settings, "Ja settings bitte umbauen", and "Auf und Zu-klapp Aktionen sind bitte immer Annimationen".

Context: the project's settings were a card of keys and values with an **Edit project** dialog. The reference edits in place, in one column, with further groups as collapsible sections. Elements folded at once, without animation, and the sidebar's groups did not fold at all: the list had the attribute `hidden`, but the rule `display: flex` of `.nav-list` overrode the browser's `display: none`, so only the chevron changed.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) One CSS mechanism for everything that folds (chosen) | `.collapse-region` for what stays in the page, `collapse-in` and `collapse-out` through `animate.enter` and `animate.leave` for what is added and removed, a rule on `<details>`, one duration and easing in tokens | One rule, one place to change it; a closed region is out of the tab order; `prefers-reduced-motion` sets the duration to 0 in one line | Grid rows instead of a height, which needs a wrapper element |
| (b) Each component animates itself | A height computed in TypeScript | No wrapper | Measuring on every toggle, and as many implementations as components |

Menus and dialogs are not folding elements and keep their behaviour. **Rationale:** a state that folds is one concept, so it has one implementation. Not verified: the animation of `<details>` where the browser has no `::details-content` (it opens at once there) and every folding element by hand; the sidebar group and the settings sections were measured in Chromium.

### Q-UI-216 · A project opens on its repositories, and a repository opens on what it holds

Status: **Decided by the owner** (2026-11-10): "Wenn ich in ein Projekt gehe, will ich zuerst die ganzen repositories im Projekt sehen. Und wenn ich auf ein Repository klicke, dann will ich nicht in die Settings des Repositories, sondern in den Inhalt des Repositories. [...] Niemand will das Repo auf dateiebene oder physikalischer ebene sehen. Es interessiert nur die logische und inhaltliche ebene.
